summary: 'In each of two rounds, I gave 48 Claude Code agents the same statistical question. No two of their texts were identical, yet every R script they wrote printed the same output whenever it was executed again. Their prose replies matched the scripts only on balanced data in the first round. In the second, run at medium effort, five of the eight scripts left to choose the analysis dropped a random slope they could have kept, and their narrower interval excluded zero. Executed code made the work repeatable and open to inspection, and it took reading that code to see why the result had changed.'
abstract: 'What happens when 48 AI agents are given the same statistical question? I tried it twice, with Claude Code agents running Claude Opus 5.5 on a simulated semantic-priming data set. Half of the agents answered in prose, without running any code, and half wrote an R script, which was then executed. Some were left to choose the analysis, and the others were told which one to run. No two agents wrote the same words, yet every script printed the same output each time it was executed under the recorded versions of R and its packages. The prose replies were patchier. In the first round, they matched the scripts on balanced data, where a mixed model can be fitted by hand, but not on unbalanced data. When the analysis was specified, they also took more than 10 times as long. In the second round, run at medium effort, not one prose reply matched an executed result. Five of the eight scripts left to choose the analysis also dropped a random slope they could have kept, which narrowed their interval enough to exclude zero. Two runs repeated at a higher effort level returned the first round''s results, a hint, though no proof, that the effort level mattered. The scripts made the work repeatable and their choices open to inspection, but they could not guarantee that the analysis was sound. I close with the evidence on how much coding literacy such checking needs, on the upkeep of code that agents write and on what experts expect of these tools over the next few years.'

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
design <- read.csv(file.path(experiment, 'design.csv'), colClasses = c(run_id = 'character'))
spec_file <- jsonlite::fromJSON(file.path(experiment, 'spec.json'))
runs_per_cell <- unique(as.vector(table(design$data, design$request, design$route)))
runs_per_cell <- runs_per_cell[runs_per_cell > 0]
stopifnot(nrow(design) == 48, length(runs_per_cell) == 1,
          sum(design$route == 'prose') * 2 == nrow(design),  # 'half of the agents answered in prose'
          spec_file$response$round == 0)  # the text says the times are whole milliseconds

# The model the agents ran, which the abstract also names
agent_model <- readLines(file.path(experiment, 'claude_model.txt'))
stopifnot(agent_model[1] == 'Claude Opus 5.5')

# Links to the experiment's files, and to the site's renv.lock, point to the
# last commit that changed them, so that a reader sees the files this page was
# built from. While they have uncommitted changes, or while that commit is on
# no branch of the remote (a rebase before pushing would give it a hash that
# GitHub never receives), or outside a git repository, the links point to master.
last_commit <- function(path) tryCatch({
  changed <- system2('git', c('status', '--porcelain', '--', path), stdout = TRUE)
  commit <- system2('git', c('log', '-1', '--format=%H', '--', path), stdout = TRUE)
  pushed <- length(commit) == 1 &&
    length(system2('git', c('branch', '--remotes', '--contains', commit), stdout = TRUE)) > 0
  if (length(changed) == 0 && pushed) commit else 'master'
}, error = function(e) 'master', warning = function(w) 'master')
experiment_ref <- last_commit(experiment)
experiment_url <- function(path = '', type = 'blob') {
  sprintf('%s/%s/%s/content/post/reproducible-research-with-generative-ai/experiment/%s',
          repo_url, type, experiment_ref, path)
}

# Counts in the prose follow APA style: words for zero to nine, numerals from
# 10 and numerals for a count set beside one of 10 or more ('3 of 16').
count_text <- function(x, compared_with = NULL) {
  words <- c('zero', 'one', 'two', 'three', 'four', 'five', 'six', 'seven',
             'eight', 'nine')
  if (x == round(x) && x >= 0 && max(c(x, compared_with)) < 10) words[x + 1]
  else format(x, big.mark = ',', scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
}
# Negative numbers in the prose and tables take a true minus sign, written as an
# HTML entity so that it survives a build in any locale. Text drawn by ggplot2
# and alt text, which knitr escapes, cannot carry the entity, so the axis of
# Figure 1 and its alt text use the character itself.
minus <- function(x) gsub('-', '&minus;', x, fixed = TRUE)
ms <- function(x, digits = 2) minus(formatC(x, format = 'f', digits = digits))
interval <- function(lower, upper, digits = 2) sprintf('[%s, %s]', ms(lower, digits), ms(upper, digits))
```

```{r figure-tools, include = FALSE}
# The figures are drawn into the page as SVG, so that their text can be selected, copied
# and found with the browser's search, and stays sharp at any zoom. svglite writes each
# figure, and the plot hook below moves it into the page, beside the narrow layout for
# phones that the figure's chunk draws with draw_narrow().

# Each colour stands for a role, which the stylesheet sets for the light and the dark
# theme (see the next chunk). In the light theme, the marks of the two routes keep the
# first and fourth colours of depictr's palette.
fig_roles <- c(ink = '#222222', muted = '#555555', grid = '#E6E6E6', rule = '#8C8C8C',
               prose = '#005B96', script = '#D55E00')
fig_roles_dark <- c(ink = '#E2E8F0', muted = '#B8C2D0', grid = '#283449', rule = '#8391A7',
                    prose = '#6CB8E6', script = '#F2914A')
stopifnot(toupper(depictr_palette(4)[c(1, 4)]) == unname(fig_roles[c('prose', 'script')]))

# Contrast as the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) define it. Text needs 4.5:1
# and graphical marks 3:1, against the page's background in each theme, and a change to
# either palette that breaks this stops the page. No text is set in the colours of the
# routes, since the vermilion reaches only 3.9:1 on white.
contrast <- function(colour, background) {
  luminance <- function(x) {
    channel <- grDevices::col2rgb(x)[, 1] / 255
    linear <- ifelse(channel <= 0.04045, channel / 12.92, ((channel + 0.055) / 1.055)^2.4)
    sum(c(0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722) * linear)
  }
  levels <- sort(c(luminance(colour), luminance(background)))
  (levels[2] + 0.05) / (levels[1] + 0.05)
}
for (theme in list(list(roles = fig_roles, background = '#FFFFFF'),
                   list(roles = fig_roles_dark, background = '#0F172A'))) {
  stopifnot(vapply(theme$roles[c('ink', 'muted')], contrast, numeric(1), background = theme$background) >= 4.5,
            vapply(theme$roles[c('rule', 'prose', 'script')], contrast, numeric(1),
                   background = theme$background) >= 3)
}

# Text is measured in the font that the page's system-ui gives on Windows, where the page
# is knitted. Other systems draw it in a font of similar width, since the SVG leaves the
# font to the page.
measure_font <- if ('Segoe UI' %in% systemfonts::system_fonts()$family) 'Segoe UI' else 'sans'
knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = 'svglite', fig.ext = 'svg',
                      dev.args = list(bg = 'transparent', fix_text_size = FALSE,
                                      system_fonts = list(sans = measure_font)))

label_size <- function(base_size) 0.88 * base_size / .pt
# Axis labels with a true minus sign
minus_labels <- function(digits = 1) {
  function(x) sub('-', '−', sprintf(paste0('%.', digits, 'f'), x), fixed = TRUE)
}
theme_figure <- function(base_size = 12) {
  theme_depictr(base_size = base_size, grid = 'x') +
    theme(text = element_text(colour = fig_roles[['ink']]),
          axis.text = element_text(colour = fig_roles[['muted']], size = rel(0.92)),
          axis.title = element_text(colour = fig_roles[['muted']], size = rel(0.92)),
          axis.title.x = element_text(margin = margin(t = 8)),
          axis.ticks = element_blank(), axis.line = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = fig_roles[['grid']], linewidth = 0.45),
          panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.background = element_blank(), plot.background = element_blank(),
          strip.background = element_blank(),
          strip.text = element_text(colour = fig_roles[['ink']], face = 'bold', hjust = 0,
                                    size = rel(0.95), margin = margin(b = 4)),
          legend.key = element_blank(), legend.background = element_blank(),
          legend.position = 'none', plot.margin = margin(6, 12, 6, 6))
}

svg_text <- function(plot, width, height) {
  previous <- grDevices::dev.cur()
  device <- svglite::svgstring(width = width, height = height, bg = 'transparent',
                               fix_text_size = FALSE, system_fonts = list(sans = measure_font))
  print(plot)
  grDevices::dev.off()
  if (previous > 1) grDevices::dev.set(previous)
  paste(device(), collapse = '\n')
}

# An SVG from svglite made to sit in the page: it scales with its column, its ids are its
# own, its colours follow the stylesheet, its text takes the page's font, and a screen
# reader announces it as one image, described by the alternative text.
web_svg <- function(svg, id, alt, layout) {
  svg <- paste(svg, collapse = '\n')
  svg <- sub('^\\s*<\\?xml[^>]*>\\s*', '', svg)
  # svglite names each clipping path after its coordinates in base64. Short names of the
  # figure's own keep the ids unique on the page and out of the spelling check.
  clip_ids <- unique(sub("^id='(.*)'$", '\\1', regmatches(svg, gregexpr("id='[^']+'", svg))[[1]]))
  for (i in seq_along(clip_ids)) {
    svg <- gsub(sprintf("id='%s'", clip_ids[i]), sprintf("id='%s-c%d'", id, i), svg, fixed = TRUE)
    svg <- gsub(sprintf('url(#%s)', clip_ids[i]), sprintf('url(#%s-c%d)', id, i), svg, fixed = TRUE)
  }
  for (role in names(fig_roles)) {
    svg <- gsub(fig_roles[[role]], sprintf('var(--fig-%s, %s)', role, fig_roles[[role]]), svg, fixed = TRUE)
  }
  svg <- gsub(' ?font-family: [^;]*;', '', svg)
  root <- regmatches(svg, regexpr('<svg [^>]*>', svg))
  stopifnot(length(root) == 1, grepl("viewBox='", root, fixed = TRUE))
  regmatches(svg, regexpr('<svg [^>]*>', svg)) <- sprintf(paste0(
    "<svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' %s class='fig-%s' role='img' aria-labelledby='%s-title'",
    " focusable='false'><title id='%s-title'>%s</title>"),
    regmatches(root, regexpr("viewBox='[^']*'", root)), layout, id, id, htmltools::htmlEscape(alt))
  svg
}

narrow_layouts <- list()
draw_narrow <- function(plot, width, height) {
  label <- knitr::opts_current$get('label')
  narrow_layouts[[label]] <<- web_svg(svg_text(plot, width, height), sprintf('fig-%s-narrow', label),
                                       knitr::opts_current$get('fig.alt'), 'narrow')
  invisible(NULL)
}
# pandoc never sees the SVG, which htmlPreserve() keeps aside until the page is written
default_plot_hook <- knitr::knit_hooks$get('plot')
knitr::knit_hooks$set(plot = function(x, options) {
  output <- default_plot_hook(x, options)
  if (!grepl('[.]svg$', x)) return(output)
  stopifnot(!is.null(narrow_layouts[[options$label]]))
  wide <- web_svg(readLines(x, warn = FALSE, encoding = 'UTF-8'), sprintf('fig-%s-wide', options$label),
                  options$fig.alt, 'wide')
  unlink(x)
  figure <- htmltools::htmlPreserve(paste0('<div class="fig-svg">', wide, narrow_layouts[[options$label]], '</div>'))
  image <- regexpr('<img [^>]*>', output)
  stopifnot(image > 0)
  regmatches(output, image) <- figure
  output
})
```

Ask a chat assistant the same statistical question twice, and you may get two different answers. A language model writes its reply one token, often a word or part of one, at a time, sampling each from a probability distribution [@holtzman2020]. That matters now that generative artificial intelligence (AI) is used at many stages of research [@andersen2025]. Reproducibility means obtaining consistent results from the same data, computational steps and conditions of analysis [@nasem2019, p. 46], and a reply in a chat window records few of those conditions.

Coding agents promise a way around this. Tools such as Claude Code can read a project, edit its files and run commands [@anthropic-overview]. When such a tool writes an R script, the model's variability enters while the script is being written. Once saved, the script can be read, tested and executed again, and given the same input, the same software environment and any random seeds it needs, it should return the same output.

I wanted to see how well that division of labour holds up, so I ran an experiment twice. In each round, `r count_text(nrow(design))` Claude Code agents received the same question about a semantic-priming data set that I had simulated with my [pilotr](/2026/pilotr-pilot-the-study-before-running-it/) package [@bernabeu2026pilotr], so the true effect was known in advance. Half of the agents answered in prose, as a chat assistant without a code interpreter would, and half wrote an R script that was then executed. Some were left to choose the analysis, and the others followed one that I specified. The results show what executing code adds to an AI-assisted analysis, and which decisions a researcher still has to check.

## Setting Up the Experiment

Before the experiment itself, it helps to see where the variation in a model's replies comes from and which of its sources a researcher can control. The next two sections review both, and the two after them describe the data and the runs. The code behind every step is folded throughout the post and can be unfolded to inspect or reproduce it.

### Why the Same Request Gets Different Replies

The obvious suspect is the randomness of sampling, which the temperature setting controls. A temperature of zero should select the most probable token at every step, yet it does not make the models that providers host deterministic. When @ouyang2025 asked ChatGPT for code several times per problem, the programs often gave different outputs, and a temperature of zero reduced that variation without removing it. @atil2025 ran five models 10 times on each of eight tasks with settings meant to be deterministic, and accuracy still varied by up to 15 percentage points across runs.

He and Thinking Machines Lab [-@he2025] traced much of this behaviour to the providers' servers, where the number of requests processed together varies with demand. That number changes the order, and so the rounding, of some sums, which can be enough to tip the choice between two almost equally probable tokens. With an open model, one that anyone can download and run, 1,000 replies to one request at temperature zero contained 80 distinct texts, and computations made independent of that number brought them down to one. Models that reason before answering are especially exposed, since an early rounding difference can send the reasoning down another path [@yuan2025].

Sampling is only one source of variation. Providers can change proprietary models at any time [@spirling2023] and retire them, after which requests to them fail [@anthropic-deprecations]. Between its March and June 2023 versions, GPT-4 fell from 84% to 51% accuracy in classifying numbers as prime or composite [@chen2024]. Meaning-preserving changes to the format of a prompt, the text given to a model, altered the accuracy of one open model by up to 76 percentage points [@sclar2024]. In a chat window, none of these sources is under the user's control, and few are recorded.

### What the Researcher Can Still Control

Reproducibility with generative AI therefore rests on three choices left to the researcher: the tools, the requests made of them and the record of both. For the tools, @mcloughlin2026 recommend open models, which can be run locally and so run again later, and, like @palmer2024, they ask that any use of a proprietary model be justified. Even an open model may not match the published one when a company serves it. In summer 2024, 11 of 31 services offering Meta's Llama models returned outputs whose distribution differed from that of the published model [@gao2025].

The choice of tools extends to their settings, such as the effort level, which sets how many tokens a model spends on reasoning, text and tool use, and whose default differs between models [@anthropic-effort]. The second round of this experiment ran at medium effort. The access route matters too, since a model may behave differently in a chat window and through an application programming interface (API), which lets other programs send it requests [@feuerriegel2026]. So does the agentic tool around the model. @nadgir2026 gave OpenAI's GPT-5.4 39 tasks that ask agents to reproduce published results from the studies' code and data. At the same effort level, it solved 94.9% of them within Codex, the company's own agentic tool, and 51.3% within CORE-Agent, an agent built for the benchmark.

A request to an agent can ask for a script in place of an answer, one that runs without manual steps, prints its result in a fixed format and sets any random seeds. It can also ask for tests of the expected behaviour and a file that pins package versions, as @bridgeford2026 recommend. What comes back still needs checking. @vangala2026 asked three coding agents for programs that would run in a clean environment, with every dependency declared. Of the 300 programs, 205 ran without intervention, and on average, they used 15 times as many packages at run time as they declared.

Asking for a script brings AI-assisted work under the standards of reproducible computational research, which ask that every result be traceable to the steps that produced it and that the versions of the software be archived [@sandve2013; see also @peng2011; @wilson2017]. A script kept under version control, in a system such as Git that records each version of a project's files, documents the steps but not the software environment. When @trisovic2022 re-executed R files deposited with published research data, 75% of those that did not time out stopped with an error, and 60% still did after automatic repairs. The renv package [@ushey2026] reduces that risk with a lockfile, which records the versions of R and of a project's packages, and the output of `sessionInfo()` shows the environment that actually ran the code.

Reporting guidelines set out the rest of the record. The GUIDE-LLM checklist asks authors in the behavioural sciences to report the provider, the exact model identifier, the date and route of access, the settings and the prompts [@feuerriegel2026]. Guidelines for software engineering add the version of the agentic tool and a trace of its tool calls, the actions it takes, such as reading a file or running a command [@baltes2026].

### A Data Set With a Known Answer

I simulated the data so that the population effect would be known. From the same specification and seed, pilotr produces identical files in R and in Python, at least for a specification such as this one, which rounds reaction times to whole milliseconds [@bernabeu2026pilotr]. In this data set, `r spec_file$units$subject$n` participants each respond to `r spec_file$units$item$n` words, once after a related prime and once after an unrelated one. The specification below sets a shifted lognormal distribution for the reaction times, a word-frequency covariate, and random intercepts and priming slopes for both participants and words.

```{r}
cat(readLines(file.path(experiment, 'spec.json')), sep = '\n')
```

The code below regenerates the data in R and compares its SHA-256 checksum, a fingerprint of the file's contents, with those of the file given to the agents and of the [file generated in Python](`r experiment_url('make_data.py')`).

```{r}
library(pilotr)

spec <- load_spec(file.path(experiment, 'spec.json'))
simulated <- simulate_design(spec)
regenerated <- data.frame(
  participant = sprintf('P%02d', simulated$subject),
  item = sprintf('W%02d', simulated$item),
  prime = simulated$prime,
  frequency = round(simulated$frequency, 2),
  rt = simulated$rt
)
# write.csv() ends each line with '\n', and a binary connection stops Windows
# from turning it into '\r\n', so the file has the same bytes on every system.
regenerated_file <- tempfile(fileext = '.csv')
connection <- file(regenerated_file, 'wb')
write.csv(regenerated, connection, row.names = FALSE, quote = FALSE)
close(connection)

checksums <- c(
  `regenerated in R` = digest::digest(file = regenerated_file, algo = 'sha256'),
  `given to the agents` = digest::digest(file = file.path(experiment, 'data.csv'), algo = 'sha256'),
  `recorded from Python` = readLines(file.path(experiment, 'python_sha256.txt'))[2]
)
stopifnot(n_distinct(checksums) == 1)
checksums
```

All `r count_text(length(checksums))` checksums match, so the three files are identical. The next calculation draws a million participants and a million words to estimate how much the priming effect varies across each in the population.

```{r}
fixed <- spec$fixed; random <- spec$random; frequency <- spec$predictors[[1]]
# effect_sd() below moves frequency with the word, so it must vary by word
stopifnot(frequency$name == 'frequency', frequency$varies_by == 'item')
mu <- fixed$intercept + fixed$coefficients$frequency * frequency$mean

# The variance, at a given prime code, of the terms that belong to one unit
# (participant or item): its random intercept and slope and their covariance.
unit_variance <- function(unit, prime_code) {
  unit$intercept_sd^2 + prime_code^2 * unit$slopes$prime_c^2 + 2 * prime_code *
    unit$intercept_sd * unit$slopes$prime_c * unit$correlations[['intercept,prime_c']]
}
residual_variance <- (fixed$coefficients$frequency * frequency$sd)^2 + spec$response$sigma^2

# The mean of a lognormal variable is exp(mu + variance / 2), and the shift
# cancels out of the difference between the two types of prime.
population_mean <- function(prime_code) {
  spec$response$shift + exp(mu + fixed$coefficients$prime_c * prime_code +
    (unit_variance(random$subject, prime_code) + unit_variance(random$item, prime_code) +
       residual_variance) / 2)
}
population_effect <- population_mean(0.5) - population_mean(-0.5)

# The priming effect of one participant (or word), averaged over the other
# unit and the residual, for a million simulated participants (or words). A
# word's frequency belongs to the word, so for words it moves with the word's
# intercept and is not averaged out.
effect_sd <- function(unit, other, word = FALSE) {
  z <- matrix(rnorm(2e6), ncol = 2)
  rho <- unit$correlations[['intercept,prime_c']]
  intercept <- unit$intercept_sd * z[, 1]
  slope <- unit$slopes$prime_c * (rho * z[, 1] + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * z[, 2])
  averaged <- residual_variance
  if (word) {
    intercept <- intercept + fixed$coefficients$frequency * frequency$sd * rnorm(nrow(z))
    averaged <- spec$response$sigma^2
  }
  unit_mean <- function(prime_code) exp(mu + intercept + prime_code * (fixed$coefficients$prime_c + slope) +
    (unit_variance(other, prime_code) + averaged) / 2)
  sd(unit_mean(0.5) - unit_mean(-0.5))
}
# The seed, that of spec.json, makes the printed standard deviations
# reproducible. Other seeds move them by a few hundredths of a millisecond,
# which leaves the one-decimal values in the text unchanged (checked below).
set.seed(2026)
effect_sds <- c(participants = effect_sd(random$subject, random$item),
                words = effect_sd(random$item, random$subject, word = TRUE))
sample_effect <- with(regenerated, mean(rt[prime == 'unrelated']) - mean(rt[prime == 'related']))
stopifnot(effect_sds[['participants']] > effect_sds[['words']])  # as the text below says

c(population_effect = population_effect, sample_effect = sample_effect,
  sd_across_participants = effect_sds[['participants']], sd_across_words = effect_sds[['words']])
```

```{r effect-sd-closed-form, include = FALSE}
# The same standard deviations in closed form. A unit's mean after either type
# of prime is lognormal, and the two exponents are jointly normal, so the
# variance of the difference follows from the variances and the covariance of
# two lognormal variables. The simulated values must round to the same decimal.
effect_sd_exact <- function(unit, other, word = FALSE) {
  frequency_variance <- if (word) (fixed$coefficients$frequency * frequency$sd)^2 else 0
  averaged <- if (word) spec$response$sigma^2 else residual_variance
  codes <- c(0.5, -0.5)
  location <- mu + codes * fixed$coefficients$prime_c + (unit_variance(other, codes) + averaged) / 2
  spread <- unit_variance(unit, codes) + frequency_variance
  covariance <- unit$intercept_sd^2 + frequency_variance - unit$slopes$prime_c^2 / 4
  variances <- exp(2 * location + spread) * (exp(spread) - 1)
  cross <- exp(sum(location) + sum(spread) / 2) * (exp(covariance) - 1)
  sqrt(sum(variances) - 2 * cross)
}
effect_sds_exact <- c(participants = effect_sd_exact(random$subject, random$item),
                      words = effect_sd_exact(random$item, random$subject, word = TRUE))
stopifnot(round(effect_sds, 1) == round(effect_sds_exact, 1))
```

In the population, responses after unrelated primes are `r ms(population_effect, 1)` ms slower than after related primes, and the effect varies more across participants (standard deviation `r ms(effect_sds[['participants']], 1)` ms) than across words (`r ms(effect_sds[['words']], 1)` ms). In the sample of `r count_text(nrow(regenerated))` trials, the difference between the mean reaction times is `r ms(sample_effect, 2)` ms.

### Forty-Eight Runs of One Question

```{r}
results <- read.csv(file.path(experiment, 'results.csv'), encoding = 'UTF-8',
                    colClasses = c(run_id = 'character'))
executions <- read.csv(file.path(experiment, 'executions.csv'), colClasses = c(run_id = 'character'))

# The logs' times are in UTC, which the format below assumes without reading
# the zone, so the zone is checked
utc_time <- function(x) {
  stopifnot(grepl('(Z|[+]00:00)$', x))
  as.POSIXct(x, format = '%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%OS', tz = 'UTC')
}
logs <- lapply(results$run_id, function(id)
  jsonlite::fromJSON(file.path(experiment, 'runs', id, 'tool_calls.json')))
results$started <- utc_time(vapply(logs, `[[`, character(1), 'started'))
results$starting_directory <- vapply(logs, `[[`, character(1), 'starting_directory')

first_date <- as.Date(min(results$started))
# Runs launched together started within a second of one another, and each
# batch at least 40 seconds after the one before, so a gap of more than 10
# seconds marks a new batch. Every batch of a round had the same size.
batch_size_of <- function(started) {
  gaps <- diff(sort(as.numeric(started)))
  size <- unique(as.vector(table(cumsum(c(TRUE, gaps > 10)))))
  stopifnot(all(gaps < 1 | gaps > 40), length(size) == 1)
  size
}
batch_size <- batch_size_of(results$started)
stopifnot(n_distinct(as.Date(results$started)) == 1)
main_runs <- results$data == 'balanced'
in_folder <- grepl('/experiment$', results$starting_directory)
in_experiment_folder <- sum(in_folder)
script_runs <- results$route == 'script'
unbalanced <- read.csv(file.path(experiment, 'data_unbalanced.csv'))

second$started <- utc_time(second$started)
second$finished <- utc_time(second$finished)
medium <- second[second$round == 'medium', ]
xhigh <- second[second$round == 'xhigh', ]
```

```{r second-round-design, include = FALSE}
# Each prompt is the first round's with three substitutions: the run's folder,

prompt_texts <- vapply(results$run_id, function(id)

second_logs <- mapply(function(round, id) {

}, second$round, second$run_id, SIMPLIFY = FALSE, USE.NAMES = FALSE)

stopifnot(is.logical(second$compliant), all(second$compliant), vapply(second_logs, function(log) {
  commands <- or_none(log$calls$input$command)
  named <- c(or_none(log$calls$input$file_path),
             unlist(regmatches(commands, gregexpr('C:/[^ "\'`;|&)]*', commands))))
  all(startsWith(named, run_folder) | startsWith(named, 'C:/Program')) &&
    !any(grepl('\\.\\./|~/|/tmp/|\\$HOME', commands))
}, logical(1)))

# The two rounds differed in date, in the version of Claude Code and in the

running_under <- function(file) {
  sub('^Running under: ', '', grep('^Running under:', readLines(file.path(experiment, file)),
                                   value = TRUE)[1])
}
second_system <- sub('^(Windows [0-9]+).*$', '\\1',
                     running_under(file.path('rerun', 'executions_session_info.txt')))
stopifnot(second_date != first_date,
          !'effort' %in% names(results),  # the first round recorded no effort level, so the text names none
          unique(second$claude_code_version) != readLines(file.path(experiment, 'claude_code_version.txt')),
          grepl('/home/user/agent_runs/', prompt_texts, fixed = TRUE),
          !grepl('/home/user/', second_prompts, fixed = TRUE), grepl('^Windows', second_system))
```

Each run received a description of the data and this question: 'How large is the priming effect, that is, how much slower are responses after unrelated primes than after related primes? Give the estimate in milliseconds with a 95% confidence interval.' It also had to end with a result line in a fixed format, so that code could compare the answers.

The request was either open, leaving the analysis to the agent, or specified, naming the model, the contrast coding and the function for the interval. Both came with the balanced data. A follow-up gave the specified request with an unbalanced version of the data, from which `r count_text(nrow(regenerated) - nrow(unbalanced))` of the `r count_text(nrow(regenerated))` trials had been removed at random. Its prompt described them as incorrect responses that had been excluded. These make up the experiment's `r count_text(nrow(unique(design[c('data', 'request')])))` conditions.

Each condition had two routes. The prose agents could read the data but were told to run no code and to approximate where necessary, as a chat assistant without a code interpreter (a tool for running code) would have to. The script agents wrote an R script, could execute it to check their work and replied with a brief summary. Their instructions named lme4 [@bates2015], lmerTest [@kuznetsova2017], emmeans and dplyr among the installed packages.

The [experiment folder](`r experiment_url(type = 'tree')`) holds the prompts, the data, the scripts, the final replies and the logs of the agents' tool calls, with a README for repeating the work, although not the agents' full transcripts. Below is the specified request as one script run received it. The open request lacks only the paragraph beginning 'Analyse the data as follows'.

```{r}
example_run <- design$run_id[design$route == 'script' & design$request == 'specified' &
                               design$data == 'balanced'][1]
cat(strwrap(readLines(file.path(experiment, 'runs', example_run, 'prompt.txt')), width = 90),
    sep = '\n')
```

Both rounds used the language model `r agent_model[1]` (identifier `r agent_model[2]`), with `r count_text(runs_per_cell)` runs in each combination of condition and route. The first round ran on `r date_text(first_date)` with Claude Code `r readLines(file.path(experiment, 'claude_code_version.txt'))`. Its `r count_text(sum(main_runs))` runs on the balanced data were launched `r count_text(batch_size)` at a time, in a random order across conditions. The `r count_text(sum(!main_runs))` runs of the follow-up were launched afterwards, also in a random order.

Each agent started in a folder of its own that held only its data file, and the logs show that the prose agents read nothing else. In the first round, however, `r count_text(sum(!results$compliant[script_runs]), sum(script_runs))` of the `r count_text(sum(script_runs))` script agents also wrote exploratory files outside their folders, although their commands show no sign of executing another agent's code. Shared temporary folders, and for some agents the experiment folder itself, were within reach, so the isolation was imperfect, and the logs and the hidden checks on this page document each exception.

Each final script was then executed `r count_text(max(executions$execution))` times, each time in a fresh R process and a fresh copy of its folder. A record kept the versions of R, lme4, lmerTest and Matrix, the package that lme4 uses for matrix computations.

The second round ran on `r date_text(second_date)` with Claude Code `r unique(second$claude_code_version)` on `r second_system`. Its `r count_text(nrow(medium))` main runs used medium effort and followed the first round's launch order, `r count_text(second_batch_size)` at a time. Their prompts changed only the folder and, for the scripts, the version of R and the path to it. I added two runs on the balanced data at xhigh effort, a prose reply to the specified request and a script for the open request. No agent of the second round touched a file outside its folder.

## Results

Unless a section names the second round, it describes the first.

### Different Words, Mostly the Same Numbers

```{r}
condition_levels <- c('Balanced data, open request', 'Balanced data, specified request',
                      'Unbalanced data, specified request')
route_levels <- c('Prose reply', 'Executed script')

text_of <- function(run_id, file) {
  paste(readLines(file.path(experiment, 'runs', run_id, file), warn = FALSE, encoding = 'UTF-8'),
        collapse = '\n')
}

runs <- results |>
  mutate(condition = factor(case_when(
           data == 'balanced' & request == 'open' ~ condition_levels[1],
           data == 'balanced' ~ condition_levels[2],
           TRUE ~ condition_levels[3]), levels = condition_levels),
         route_label = factor(ifelse(route == 'prose', route_levels[1], route_levels[2]),
                              levels = route_levels),
         reply = vapply(run_id, text_of, character(1), file = 'response.txt'),
         text = mapply(function(id, rte) text_of(id, if (rte == 'script') 'analysis.R' else 'response.txt'),
                       run_id, route))

# The numbers of each RESULT line as written, so that a reply's precision is
# kept (a reply's '22.0' is not the same claim as a script's '21.79')
result_numbers <- function(line) {
  regmatches(line, regexec('estimate=(-?[0-9.]+) lower=(-?[0-9.]+) upper=(-?[0-9.]+)', line))[[1]][-1]
}
# Each result line as the tables show it, 'estimate [lower, upper]'
as_written <- function(lines) {
  vapply(lines, function(line) {
    n <- result_numbers(line)
    sprintf('%s [%s, %s]', minus(n[1]), minus(n[2]), minus(n[3]))
  }, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
}
runs$result_text <- as_written(runs$result_line)

# The paired differences (unrelated minus related) in the balanced data, and
# each participant's and each word's mean difference
balanced <- read.csv(file.path(experiment, 'data.csv'))
paired <- reshape(balanced[, c('participant', 'item', 'prime', 'rt')],
                  idvar = c('participant', 'item'), timevar = 'prime', direction = 'wide')
paired$difference <- paired$rt.unrelated - paired$rt.related
# reshape() would keep only the first of any repeated trial, and a pair with a
# trial missing would leave a missing difference, so neither must occur
stopifnot(nrow(paired) * 2 == nrow(balanced), !anyNA(paired$difference))
participant_means <- tapply(paired$difference, paired$participant, mean)
word_means <- tapply(paired$difference, paired$item, mean)
# The by-participant paired t interval, which most open-request replies mention
paired_ci <- t.test(participant_means)$conf.int

summary_table <- runs |>
  group_by(condition, route_label) |>
  summarise(distinct_texts = n_distinct(text),
            distinct_results = n_distinct(result_line),
            result = first(result_text), .groups = 'drop')
```

```{r facts, include = FALSE}
# The prose below describes the pattern these checks confirm. If new data broke
# the pattern, the page would stop building here instead of describing results
# that no longer hold.
first_of <- function(cond, rte) runs |> filter(condition == cond, route == rte) |> slice(1)
open_script <- first_of(condition_levels[1], 'script')
specified_script <- first_of(condition_levels[2], 'script')
unbalanced_script <- first_of(condition_levels[3], 'script')
unbalanced_prose <- runs |> filter(condition == condition_levels[3], route == 'prose') |> arrange(order)
stopifnot(!is.unsorted(unbalanced_prose$started))  # Table 3 numbers the replies in launch order

# A prose number agrees with a script's when the script's number, rounded to
# the decimals the prose wrote, equals it. The decimals are counted in the text
# of the RESULT line, since '22.0' read as a number would lose its trailing zero.
decimals <- function(text) ifelse(grepl('.', text, fixed = TRUE), nchar(sub('^[^.]*\\.', '', text)), 0L)
# Each number of a result line minus the script's, once the latter is rounded
# to the decimals of the former. The difference is rounded to six decimals, so
# that floating-point error cannot make equal numbers differ.
difference_at_precision <- function(line, script) {
  written <- result_numbers(line)
  round(as.numeric(written) - round(c(script$estimate, script$lower, script$upper), decimals(written)), 6)
}
compare <- function(prose, script) sign(difference_at_precision(prose$result_line, script))
agrees <- function(prose, script) all(compare(prose, script) == 0)
# Rounding a script's two-decimal number to the one decimal of a reply is
# unambiguous only when its second decimal is not 5
stopifnot(round(abs(unlist(results[results$route == 'script', c('estimate', 'lower', 'upper')])) * 100) %% 10 != 5)
balanced_prose <- runs |> filter(route == 'prose', data == 'balanced')
balanced_agreement <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(balanced_prose)), function(i) {
  script <- if (balanced_prose$request[i] == 'open') open_script else specified_script
  agrees(balanced_prose[i, ], script)
}, logical(1))
unbalanced_signs <- t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(unbalanced_prose)), function(i)
  compare(unbalanced_prose[i, ], unbalanced_script), numeric(3)))
unbalanced_agreement <- rowSums(unbalanced_signs != 0) == 0

identical_stored <- executions |> group_by(run_id) |> summarise(identical = n_distinct(stdout_sha256) == 1)

stopifnot(
  !anyNA(results[c('estimate', 'lower', 'upper')]),
  n_distinct(runs$text) == nrow(runs),
  all(summary_table$distinct_results[summary_table$route_label == route_levels[2]] == 1),
  all(summary_table$distinct_results[summary_table$condition != condition_levels[3]] == 1),
  all(balanced_agreement),
  !any(unbalanced_agreement),
  all(unbalanced_signs[, 2] > 0),
  any(unbalanced_signs[, 3] > 0), any(unbalanced_signs[, 3] < 0),
  all(results$compliant[results$route == 'prose']),
  all(identical_stored$identical),
  all(executions$status == 0),
  # every script was executed the number of times the text gives
  setequal(executions$run_id, runs$run_id[runs$route == 'script']),
  all(table(executions$run_id) == max(executions$execution))
)

# What the instructions for each route said, as the design describes them
# (prompt_texts holds the first round's prompts, read with the second round's)
stopifnot(grepl('If you cannot compute the answer exactly, give your best estimate.',
                prompt_texts[!script_runs], fixed = TRUE),
          grepl('packages that include lme4, lmerTest, emmeans and dplyr', prompt_texts[script_runs],
                fixed = TRUE),
          # and asked each script run for the summary that the text describes
          grepl('reply with a brief summary of what it does', prompt_texts[script_runs], fixed = TRUE),
          # and for an R script that reads the data. As the text says, the script
          # must end by printing a fixed result line and work only inside its
          # folder
          grepl('Write an R script named analysis.R in that directory that reads data.csv',
                prompt_texts[script_runs], fixed = TRUE),
          grepl('The last line the script prints must have exactly this form', prompt_texts[script_runs],
                fixed = TRUE),
          grepl('Work only inside that directory', prompt_texts[script_runs], fixed = TRUE),
          # and told each prose run to use no tool but the one that reads the data
          grepl('use no other tool', prompt_texts[!script_runs], fixed = TRUE))

# The isolation the design describes, from the logs. Every prose run read its
# own data file and nothing else, and no run named the experiment's folder, its
# specification, a parent directory or the home directory. The runs launched
# from that folder were the first, named no file outside their own directory
# and began every command by changing to it, or read a background task's
# output in /tmp. The script runs that left their directory wrote and ran each
# file in the session's scratch folder within one command, working from their
# own directory or naming their own data file, and one of them also read from
# the session's task folder.
own_dir <- file.path('/home/user/agent_runs', results$run_id)
calls_text <- vapply(logs, function(log) as.character(jsonlite::toJSON(log$calls)), character(1))
outside <- unlist(strsplit(results$outside_paths[script_runs & !results$compliant], ' '))
stopifnot(mapply(function(log, dir) all(log$calls$tool == 'Read') &&
                   all(log$calls$input$file_path == file.path(dir, 'data.csv')),
                 logs[!script_runs], own_dir[!script_runs]),
          !any(grepl('website-files|/experiment\\b|spec\\.json|\\.\\./|~/|\\$HOME', calls_text)),
          max(results$started[in_folder]) < min(results$started[!in_folder]),
          grepl('/(scratchpad|tasks)/[^/]+$', outside),
          sum(grepl('/tasks/', results$outside_paths)) == 1)
for (i in which(in_folder)) {
  input <- logs[[i]]$calls$input
  commands <- or_none(input$command)
  files <- or_none(input$file_path)
  stopifnot(startsWith(files, own_dir[i]),
            startsWith(commands, paste('cd', own_dir[i])) | grepl('^(sleep [0-9]+; )?cat /tmp/', commands))
}
for (i in which(script_runs & !results$compliant)) {
  scratch <- grep('scratchpad/', na.omit(logs[[i]]$calls$input$command), value = TRUE)
  written <- regmatches(scratch, regexpr('(?<=cat > )\\S+scratchpad/\\S+\\.R', scratch, perl = TRUE))
  # each such run wrote at least one file outside its folder, as the text says
  stopifnot(length(written) > 0, length(written) == length(scratch),
            mapply(function(file, command) grepl(paste('Rscript', file), command, fixed = TRUE),
                   written, scratch),
            startsWith(scratch, paste('cd', own_dir[i])) |
              grepl(file.path(own_dir[i], 'data.csv'), scratch, fixed = TRUE))
}

# The follow-up was launched after the main runs, while some of them were
# still running, as the text on the time taken says. It was therefore designed
# before every result on the balanced data was in, as the Limits say.
finished <- utc_time(vapply(logs, `[[`, character(1), 'finished'))
followup_after_main <- min(results$started[!main_runs]) > max(results$started[main_runs])
main_still_running <- sum(finished[main_runs] > min(results$started[!main_runs]))
stopifnot(followup_after_main, main_still_running > 0)

choices <- read.csv(file.path(experiment, 'choices_open_scripts.csv'), colClasses = c(run_id = 'character'))
stopifnot(setequal(choices$run_id, runs$run_id[runs$condition == condition_levels[1] &
                                                  runs$route == 'script']),
          n_distinct(choices$final_random_effects) == 1,
          n_distinct(choices$interval_method) == 1,
          # as the text describes them: no by-participant slope,
          # Satterthwaite intervals, untransformed times and every trial kept
          unique(choices$final_random_effects) == '(1 | participant) + (1 + prime | item)',
          unique(choices$interval_method) == 'Satterthwaite t',
          all(choices$transformation == 'none'), all(choices$exclusions == 'none'))

# The Satterthwaite interval of a model's priming effect, from lmerTest
satterthwaite_ci <- function(fit) {
  coefficients <- summary(fit)$coefficients['prime_c', ]
  coefficients[['Estimate']] + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, coefficients[['df']]) * coefficients[['Std. Error']]
}
# The coded choices, checked against the scripts themselves: the model without
# by-participant slopes gives the scripts' Satterthwaite interval, and the
# scripts coded as including word frequency are those whose formula adds it to
# the prime (a check that relies on their shared name for it, freq_c)
open_texts <- runs$text[match(choices$run_id, runs$run_id)]
reduced_check <- lmerTest::lmer(rt ~ prime_c + (1 | participant) + (1 + prime_c | item),
                                data = transform(balanced, prime_c = ifelse(prime == 'unrelated', 0.5, -0.5)))
stopifnot(round(satterthwaite_ci(reduced_check), 2) == c(open_script$lower, open_script$upper),
          grepl('rt ~ prime_c + freq_c', open_texts, fixed = TRUE) == choices$frequency_covariate)

# The packages the agents' scripts load, named in the text
script_texts <- runs$text[runs$route == 'script']
packages_loaded <- sort(unique(unlist(regmatches(script_texts,
  gregexpr('(?<=library\\()[A-Za-z0-9.]+(?=\\))|[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9.]*(?=::)', script_texts, perl = TRUE)))))
packages_loaded <- setdiff(packages_loaded, c('base', 'stats', 'utils', 'methods'))
# The scripts that compute Kenward-Roger degrees of freedom, for which lmerTest
# calls pbkrtest
kenward_scripts <- sum(grepl('"Kenward-Roger"', script_texts, fixed = TRUE))
stopifnot(kenward_scripts > 0, c('lme4', 'lmerTest') %in% packages_loaded,
          # 'open-request scripts that also report Kenward-Roger', beside the
          # Satterthwaite interval that the checks of choices above confirm
          all(runs$request[runs$route == 'script'][grepl('"Kenward-Roger"', script_texts, fixed = TRUE)] == 'open'))

unbalanced_raw_difference <- with(unbalanced, mean(rt[prime == 'unrelated']) - mean(rt[prime == 'related']))
# Participant-word pairs left with a trial after only one type of prime, or
# after neither, once trials were removed
pairs_kept <- table(unbalanced$participant, unbalanced$item)
pairs_one_prime <- sum(pairs_kept == 1)
pairs_no_trial <- sum(pairs_kept == 0)
stopifnot(pairs_one_prime > 0, pairs_no_trial > 0,
          length(pairs_kept) == nrow(paired))  # every participant and word remains

# The largest distance of each reply's three numbers from the executed ones as
# the scripts printed them, to two decimals, without rounding those to the
# reply's precision as Figure 1 does, since the replies' stated margins refer
# to the exact values
largest_discrepancy <- with(unbalanced_prose, pmax(abs(estimate - unbalanced_script$estimate),
                                                   abs(lower - unbalanced_script$lower),
                                                   abs(upper - unbalanced_script$upper)))
hedged <- sum(grepl('approximat|by hand|hand calculation|hand estimate', unbalanced_prose$reply,
                    ignore.case = TRUE))
stopifnot(hedged == nrow(unbalanced_prose))

# The margin each reply to the unbalanced data gave for its numbers, coded
# from the phrase quoted, which must appear in the reply. 'A few tenths' of a
# millisecond is coded as 0.5 ms, for the bounds as well as the estimate
# (where two replies allowed 'slightly more' or 'a little more'), and a margin
# given only for the estimate is applied to the bounds as well. Where a reply
# gave the estimate a margin of its own, estimate_phrase quotes it, and
# otherwise repeats phrase. Every margin is wider than the discrepancy it
# covers, as the text says.
stated_margins <- tibble::tribble(
  ~run_id,    ~phrase,                                         ~estimate_phrase,                                  ~estimate, ~bounds,
  'a42064f2', 'treat the estimate as ±0.5 ms',                 'treat the estimate as ±0.5 ms',                   0.5,       0.5,
  'c3d30006', 'off by up to about 0.5 ms',                     'off by up to about 0.5 ms',                       0.5,       0.5,
  '6a3dce23', '1–2 ms for the interval ends',                  'off by up to about 0.5 ms for the estimate',      0.5,       2,
  '910f595d', 'a few tenths of a millisecond on the estimate', 'a few tenths of a millisecond on the estimate',   0.5,       0.5,
  'c3db0267', 'a few tenths of a millisecond in the estimate', 'a few tenths of a millisecond in the estimate',   0.5,       0.5,
  'cfe8d155', 'within a few tenths of a millisecond',          'within a few tenths of a millisecond',            0.5,       0.5,
  '777b32fe', 'each CI bound within about ±2 ms',              'estimate should be within about ±0.5 ms',         0.5,       2,
  'ce585f0c', 'could be off by 1–3 ms',                        'point estimate is probably within about ±0.5 ms', 0.5,       3)
stated_margins <- stated_margins[match(unbalanced_prose$run_id, stated_margins$run_id), ]
stopifnot(!anyNA(stated_margins$run_id),
          mapply(grepl, stated_margins$phrase, unbalanced_prose$reply, fixed = TRUE),
          mapply(grepl, stated_margins$estimate_phrase, unbalanced_prose$reply, fixed = TRUE),
          abs(unbalanced_prose$estimate - unbalanced_script$estimate) < stated_margins$estimate,
          abs(unbalanced_prose$lower - unbalanced_script$lower) < stated_margins$bounds,
          abs(unbalanced_prose$upper - unbalanced_script$upper) < stated_margins$bounds,
          unbalanced_prose$lower > unbalanced_script$lower)

# The replies that noted how close the lower bound lay to zero, and those that
# added that whether it excluded zero depended on their precision
near_zero <- grepl('(just|close to)[^.]{0,25}zero|borderline|marginal', unbalanced_prose$reply,
                   ignore.case = TRUE, perl = TRUE)
depends_on_precision <- grepl('itself approximate|depends on (that precision|the exact)',
                              unbalanced_prose$reply)
stopifnot(sum(near_zero) > nrow(unbalanced_prose) / 2, any(depends_on_precision),
          all(near_zero[depends_on_precision]))

# The model the replies to the unbalanced data approximated. Each put the
# by-participant slope variance at or near zero (the phrase quoted must appear
# in the reply), none placed it at the boundary with a correlation of +1, as
# lme4 does, and their numbers lie closer to the model without by-participant
# slopes, whose lower bound also lies above the executed one, than to the
# executed result. The same model with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, as the
# open-request scripts computed their intervals, gives an interval that,
# unlike the Wald one, includes zero.
unbalanced$prime_c <- ifelse(unbalanced$prime == 'unrelated', 0.5, -0.5)
unbalanced_fit <- lmerTest::lmer(rt ~ prime_c + (1 + prime_c | participant) + (1 + prime_c | item),
                                 data = unbalanced)
unbalanced_participant <- lme4::VarCorr(unbalanced_fit)$participant
unbalanced_reduced <- lme4::lmer(rt ~ prime_c + (1 | participant) + (1 + prime_c | item),
                                 data = unbalanced)
reduced_numbers <- c(lme4::fixef(unbalanced_reduced)[['prime_c']],
                     confint(unbalanced_reduced, parm = 'prime_c', method = 'Wald'))
prose_numbers <- as.matrix(unbalanced_prose[c('estimate', 'lower', 'upper')])
executed_numbers <- c(unbalanced_script$estimate, unbalanced_script$lower, unbalanced_script$upper)
participant_zero <- c(
  a42064f2 = 'participant slope variance at about zero',
  c3d30006 = 'comes out at zero or slightly below',
  `6a3dce23` = 'By-participant slope variance: about 0',
  `910f595d` = 'random-slope variance should therefore come out at or near zero',
  c3db0267 = 'estimate this variance at or near zero',
  cfe8d155 = 'by-participant slope variance at or near zero',
  `777b32fe` = 'slope variance:** about zero',
  ce585f0c = 'participant slope variance comes out negative')
unbalanced_satterthwaite <- satterthwaite_ci(unbalanced_fit)
stopifnot(setequal(names(participant_zero), unbalanced_prose$run_id),
          mapply(grepl, participant_zero[unbalanced_prose$run_id], unbalanced_prose$reply, fixed = TRUE),
          !any(grepl('\\+ ?1\\b|perfectly correlated', unbalanced_prose$reply)),
          lme4::isSingular(unbalanced_fit),
          round(attr(unbalanced_participant, 'correlation')[1, 2], 3) == 1,
          # every reply, not only all of them together
          all(rowSums(abs(sweep(prose_numbers, 2, reduced_numbers))) <
                rowSums(abs(sweep(prose_numbers, 2, executed_numbers)))),
          reduced_numbers[2] > unbalanced_script$lower,
          unbalanced_script$lower > 0, unbalanced_satterthwaite[1] < 0)

minutes_of <- function(cond, rte) median(runs$minutes[runs$condition == cond & runs$route == rte])
# The text gives one median for the scripts given the specified request, so it
# is computed over both of its conditions
specified_script_runs <- runs$route == 'script' & runs$request == 'specified'
specified_script_minutes <- median(runs$minutes[specified_script_runs])
# The open request took the scripts more tool calls than the specified one, and
# every prose reply to the specified request took over 10 times as long as any
# script, as the abstract says
open_tool_calls <- median(runs$tool_calls[runs$condition == condition_levels[1] & runs$route == 'script'])
specified_tool_calls <- median(runs$tool_calls[specified_script_runs])
stopifnot(min(runs$tool_calls[runs$condition == condition_levels[1] & runs$route == 'script']) >
            max(runs$tool_calls[specified_script_runs]),
          min(runs$minutes[runs$route == 'prose' & runs$request == 'specified']) >
            10 * max(runs$minutes[specified_script_runs]))
# How long each stored execution of a specified script took, R's start-up included
specified_seconds <- executions$seconds[executions$run_id %in% runs$run_id[specified_script_runs]]
# How far the prose replies to the unbalanced data lay from one another
reply_spread <- max(vapply(unbalanced_prose[c('estimate', 'lower', 'upper')],
                           function(x) diff(range(x)), numeric(1)))

# A number is mentioned when it appears, written to one or two decimals, with
# no digit, decimal point or comma before it and no digit after it.
mentions <- function(value, text) {
  forms <- unique(c(sprintf('%.1f', value), sprintf('%.2f', value)))
  patterns <- sprintf('(?<![0-9.,])%s(?![0-9])', gsub('.', '\\.', forms, fixed = TRUE))
  Reduce(`|`, lapply(patterns, grepl, x = text, perl = TRUE))
}
open_runs <- runs |> filter(condition == condition_levels[1])
# The open-request runs that mentioned the by-participant interval, by route:
# every prose reply did, and the summaries of some of the scripts
noted_paired <- mentions(paired_ci[1], open_runs$reply) & mentions(paired_ci[2], open_runs$reply)
noted_by_route <- tapply(noted_paired, open_runs$route, sum)
stopifnot(noted_by_route[['prose']] == runs_per_cell)
# Every open-request run that mentioned the by-participant interval set it
# aside for ignoring the variation across words, and every reply to the
# unbalanced data weighted the per-word effects, as the text says
set_aside <- sprintf('ignor|treats? the %d words|only words that matter|overstat|too narrow|sample too',
                     spec_file$units$item$n)
stopifnot(all(grepl(set_aside, open_runs$reply[noted_paired], ignore.case = TRUE)),
          all(grepl('weight', unbalanced_prose$reply, ignore.case = TRUE)))

# The replies to the open request that equated their decomposition with the
# maximal model, coded from the phrase quoted, which must appear in the reply
equated_maximal <- tibble::tribble(
  ~run_id,    ~phrase,
  'ecd10c31', 'and a priming slope for each, does with balanced data',
  'ccaff99f', '(1 + prime | participant) + (1 + prime | item)',
  'deb8444d', 'a mixed model with crossed random effects and prime slopes for both',
  'd2aba3cb', 'model with random prime slopes for both',
  '469f84cf', 'crossed random participant and item effects on the priming effect would give')
stopifnot(mapply(function(id, phrase) grepl(phrase, runs$reply[runs$run_id == id], fixed = TRUE),
                 equated_maximal$run_id, equated_maximal$phrase),
          equated_maximal$run_id %in% open_runs$run_id[open_runs$route == 'prose'])
# A check on wording only: no other prose reply to the open request speaks of
# slopes for both units or of the maximal model. It would miss a reply that
# equated the two in other words. cdc86c2c's 'prime slopes for participants and
# words' describes the model behind the same estimate, not the decomposition,
# and is rightly not listed.
other_open_prose <- open_runs$reply[open_runs$route == 'prose' & !open_runs$run_id %in% equated_maximal$run_id]
stopifnot(!any(grepl('slopes? for (both|each)|both .{0,30}slopes|[|] ?participant[)]|maximal',
                     other_open_prose, perl = TRUE)))

# The maximal model with the Satterthwaite interval of the open-request scripts
# gives a wider interval than the model without by-participant slopes, and its
# Wald interval, which the specified request asked for, is narrower than both
maximal_fit <- lmerTest::lmer(rt ~ prime_c + (1 + prime_c | participant) + (1 + prime_c | item),
                              data = transform(balanced, prime_c = ifelse(prime == 'unrelated', 0.5, -0.5)))
maximal_ci <- satterthwaite_ci(maximal_fit)
stopifnot(maximal_ci[1] < open_script$lower, maximal_ci[2] > open_script$upper,
          specified_script$upper - specified_script$lower < open_script$upper - open_script$lower)

# The standard deviations of the priming effect across participants and words
# that the maximal model estimates from the sample, which the text says reverse
# the order of those in the population (effect_sds)
sample_sds <- c(participants = attr(lme4::VarCorr(maximal_fit)$participant, 'stddev')[['prime_c']],
                words = attr(lme4::VarCorr(maximal_fit)$item, 'stddev')[['prime_c']])
stopifnot(sample_sds[['participants']] < sample_sds[['words']],
          effect_sds[['participants']] > effect_sds[['words']])

# The discussion says that the specified request names R functions and code,
# that every script given it computed the Wald interval of the maximal model
# and that no run given it mentioned Satterthwaite or Kenward-Roger degrees of
# freedom
specified_prompts <- prompt_texts[results$request == 'specified']
specified_runs <- runs |> filter(request == 'specified')
stopifnot(grepl('lme4::lmer()', specified_prompts, fixed = TRUE),
          grepl('rt ~ prime_c + (1 + prime_c | participant) + (1 + prime_c | item)', specified_prompts,
                fixed = TRUE),
          grepl('confint(fit, parm = "prime_c", method = "Wald")', specified_prompts, fixed = TRUE),
          round(confint(maximal_fit, parm = 'prime_c', method = 'Wald'), 2) ==
            c(specified_script$lower, specified_script$upper),
          round(confint(unbalanced_fit, parm = 'prime_c', method = 'Wald'), 2) ==
            c(unbalanced_script$lower, unbalanced_script$upper),
          !grepl('Satterthwaite|Kenward', c(specified_runs$reply, specified_runs$text), ignore.case = TRUE))

# The contrasts the text draws: the effect varies less across participants than
# across words in the sample, the by-participant interval excludes zero while
# the mixed models' intervals include it (and the population effect) until
# trials are removed, the by-word test reproduces the open-request scripts'
# interval, the model's estimate equals the difference in means only with
# balance, and the open request took the scripts longer than the specified one
stopifnot(sd(participant_means) < sd(word_means), paired_ci[1] > 0,
          open_script$lower < 0, specified_script$lower < 0, unbalanced_script$lower > 0,
          open_script$lower < population_effect, population_effect < open_script$upper,
          specified_script$lower < population_effect, population_effect < specified_script$upper,
          all(round(t.test(word_means)$conf.int, 2) == c(open_script$lower, open_script$upper)),
          round(sample_effect, 2) == specified_script$estimate,
          round(sample_effect, 2) == open_script$estimate,
          round(unbalanced_raw_difference, 2) != unbalanced_script$estimate,
          minutes_of(condition_levels[1], 'script') > specified_script_minutes)
# The Limits say that the lower bound of the interval lay close to zero:
# in every condition, within a twentieth of the interval's width
executed_lower <- c(open_script$lower, specified_script$lower, unbalanced_script$lower)
executed_upper <- c(open_script$upper, specified_script$upper, unbalanced_script$upper)
stopifnot(abs(executed_lower) < (executed_upper - executed_lower) / 20)

# Every summary of an open-request script reported the dropped by-participant
# slope and justified it by the fit of the maximal model, as the discussion says
open_script_replies <- runs$reply[runs$condition == condition_levels[1] & runs$route == 'script']
stopifnot(all(grepl('drop|steps down', open_script_replies) |
                grepl('(1 | participant)', open_script_replies, fixed = TRUE)),
          all(grepl('singular|degenerate|boundary|fit properly|settle properly|about zero|essentially zero',
                    open_script_replies, ignore.case = TRUE)))

# How far each of the three numbers that ended a run lay from those of the
# executed scripts in the same condition, at the precision the run wrote it: the
# scripts' number is rounded to the decimals of the run's, as in agrees() above
number_levels <- c('Estimate', 'Lower bound', 'Upper bound')
deviations <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(runs)), function(i) {
  data.frame(run_id = runs$run_id[i], condition = runs$condition[i], route_label = runs$route_label[i],
             number = factor(number_levels, levels = number_levels),
             deviation = difference_at_precision(runs$result_line[i], first_of(runs$condition[i], 'script')))
}))
unbalanced_prose_deviations <- deviations$deviation[deviations$condition == condition_levels[3] &
                                                      deviations$route_label == route_levels[1]]
# Figure 1 and the text describe this pattern: every number of every script, and
# every reply to the balanced data, agrees at its precision, and the replies to
# the unbalanced data do not
stopifnot(all(deviations$deviation[deviations$route_label == route_levels[2]] == 0),
          all(deviations$deviation[deviations$condition != condition_levels[3]] == 0),
          any(unbalanced_prose_deviations != 0))

# The captions and alternative text of Figures 1 and 2, from the same data. The
# differences in the alternative text take a true minus sign, since knitr escapes the
# entity there.
executed_result <- function(script) {
  sprintf('%s %s ms', ms(script$estimate), interval(script$lower, script$upper))
}
cap_estimates <- sprintf(paste(
  'How Far the First Round\'s Prose Replies to the Unbalanced Data Lay From the Executed Result.',
  'Each dot is one of the %s replies, placed at its number minus that of the scripts, once the scripts\' number is',
  'rounded to the decimals the reply wrote, and dots that would overlap are stacked. The vertical line marks the',
  'executed result, %s, which all %s scripts printed. All %d runs on the balanced data, prose and scripts alike,',
  'agreed with the executed result at the precision they reported.'),
  count_text(nrow(unbalanced_prose)), executed_result(unbalanced_script), count_text(runs_per_cell),
  sum(runs$data == 'balanced'))
cap_minutes <- sprintf(paste(
  'Minutes From Request to Final Reply in the %d Runs of the First Round. Each point is one run, spread',
  'vertically within its route so that runs with similar times stay visible, and the tick and number mark the',
  'median of each route. Equal distances on the logarithmic axis stand for equal ratios, and the times include',
  'waiting for the shared service.'), nrow(runs))

signed <- function(x) sub('-', '−', format(x), fixed = TRUE)
unbalanced_lower_deviations <- deviations$deviation[deviations$condition == condition_levels[3] &
                                                      deviations$route_label == route_levels[1] &
                                                      deviations$number == 'Lower bound']
alt_estimates <- sprintf(paste(
  'Dot plot in three panels, for the estimate and the two bounds of the interval. Each panel shows the %s',
  'prose replies to the unbalanced data as dots placed at their difference from the executed result, which a',
  'vertical line marks at zero. The differences range from %s to %s ms, and every lower bound lies above the',
  'executed one, by %s to %s ms.'),
  count_text(nrow(unbalanced_prose)),
  signed(min(unbalanced_prose_deviations)), signed(max(unbalanced_prose_deviations)),
  signed(min(unbalanced_lower_deviations)), signed(max(unbalanced_lower_deviations)))
stopifnot(all(unbalanced_lower_deviations > 0))  # 'every lower bound lies above the executed one'

# The range of the minutes of a route, in all conditions or in some. Ranges of
# run times are written with one decimal below 10 minutes and none above.
# Medians and single-run times keep one decimal, as in Table 4.
range_in <- function(rte, conditions = condition_levels) {
  range(runs$minutes[runs$route == rte & runs$condition %in% conditions])
}
minutes_text <- function(x) ifelse(x < 10, sprintf('%.1f', x), sprintf('%.0f', x))
specified_conditions <- condition_levels[2:3]
# The text and the alt text say that, with the open request, the times of the
# two routes overlapped
stopifnot(range_in('script', condition_levels[1])[2] > range_in('prose', condition_levels[1])[1],
          range_in('script', condition_levels[1])[1] < range_in('prose', condition_levels[1])[2])
alt_minutes <- sprintf(paste(
  'Dot plot of the minutes each run took, on a logarithmic axis, with one panel for each condition and',
  'separate rows for prose replies and executed scripts. Each row has %s points and a labelled median.',
  'With the specified request, the scripts',
  'took %s to %s minutes and the prose replies %s to %s. With the open request, the times of the two',
  'routes overlapped.'),
  count_text(runs_per_cell), minutes_text(range_in('script', specified_conditions)[1]), minutes_text(range_in('script', specified_conditions)[2]),
  minutes_text(range_in('prose', specified_conditions)[1]), minutes_text(range_in('prose', specified_conditions)[2]))
```

All `r count_text(nrow(runs))` texts differed, as long generated texts will, but their results agreed far more closely (Table 1). On the balanced data, the `r count_text(runs_per_cell)` runs of each route reported the same result in each condition, and the prose replies agreed with the executed scripts to the precision they gave. On the unbalanced data, the `r count_text(runs_per_cell)` scripts again printed a single result, whereas the prose replies gave `r count_text(n_distinct(unbalanced_prose$result_line))` different results, none of which matched the scripts. Figure 1 shows how far each of those replies lay from the executed result, in the theme and colours of my [depictr](/2026/depictr-one-visual-language-from-first-look-to-final-figure/) package [@bernabeu2026depictr].

```{r}
# The result is shown where every run in the row reported the same one. The
# checks above allow more than one only in the prose replies to the unbalanced data

# Pandoc sizes the columns of a wide table in proportion to the dashes under
# its header, which kable counts from the longest cell, markup included. Where
# that misjudges a column, the dashes are set to fixed percentages of the
# width instead. Here the six characters of each &nbsp; would widen the
# column of routes, so the shares are those pandoc gave this table without them.
column_shares <- function(table, shares) {
  separator <- grep('^\\|[-:|]+\\|$', table)
  cells <- strsplit(sub('^\\|(.*)\\|$', '\\1', table[separator]), '|', fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
  stopifnot(length(separator) == 1, length(cells) == length(shares), sum(shares) == 100)
  table[separator] <- paste0('|', paste0(ifelse(startsWith(cells, ':'), ':', ''), strrep('-', shares),
                                         ifelse(endsWith(cells, ':'), ':', ''), collapse = '|'), '|')
  table
}

column_shares(knitr::kable(
  summary_table |>
    arrange(condition, desc(route_label)) |>
    # A route's two words stay together, so that both routes take one line
    transmute(Condition = condition, Route = gsub(' ', '&nbsp;', route_label, fixed = TRUE),
              `Distinct texts` = distinct_texts, `Distinct results` = distinct_results,
              `Estimate [95% interval] (ms)` = if_else(distinct_results == 1, result, 'See Table 3')),
  caption = sprintf(paste(
    'Texts and Results of the First Round in Each Condition and Route. Each row covers %s runs. The texts are the',
    'replies in the prose route and the scripts in the script route. A result is the estimate and interval',
    'in a run\'s result line, as the run wrote it, and is shown when every run in the row reported the',
    'same one.'), count_text(runs_per_cell)),
  align = c('l', 'l', 'r', 'r', 'r')), shares = c(32, 14, 13, 15, 26))
```

```{r estimates, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 2.5, fig.cap = cap_estimates, fig.alt = alt_estimates}
# deviations, built with the hidden checks earlier on the page, holds each of the three
# numbers of every run minus the executed scripts' number in its condition, once the
# latter is rounded to the decimals the run wrote. Every script, and every run on the
# balanced data, lies at zero, so the figure plots the prose replies to the unbalanced
# data against a line at zero for the executed result.

# Dots closer than the gap, about the width of a dot, stack upwards, so that every run
# stays visible
stack_levels <- function(x, gap) {
  levels <- integer(length(x))
  for (i in seq_along(x)) {
    taken <- levels[seq_len(i - 1)][abs(x[seq_len(i - 1)] - x[i]) < gap]
    level <- 0L
    while (level %in% taken) level <- level + 1L
    levels[i] <- level
  }
  levels
}

fig_deviations <- function(narrow = FALSE, base_size = if (narrow) 12 else 11) {
  dots <- deviations |>
    filter(condition == condition_levels[3], route_label == route_levels[1]) |>
    group_by(number) |> arrange(deviation, .by_group = TRUE) |>
    mutate(level = stack_levels(deviation, gap = 0.035)) |> ungroup()
  top <- max(dots$level) + 1.9
  first_panel <- factor(levels(dots$number)[1], levels = levels(dots$number))
  notes <- data.frame(number = first_panel,
                      x = c(0.012, max(dots$deviation[dots$number == first_panel]) + 0.045),
                      y = c(top - 0.35, 0.15),
                      label = c(sprintf('Executed result,\nall %s scripts', count_text(runs_per_cell)),
                                sprintf('%s prose\nreplies', stringr::str_to_sentence(count_text(nrow(unbalanced_prose))))),
                      colour = c('ink', 'muted'))
  ggplot(dots, aes(deviation, level)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = fig_roles[['script']], linewidth = 1.1) +
    geom_point(colour = fig_roles[['prose']], size = 2.6, shape = 16) +
    geom_text(aes(x, y, label = label), data = notes, inherit.aes = FALSE, hjust = 0, vjust = c(1, 0),
              lineheight = 0.95, size = label_size(base_size), colour = fig_roles[notes$colour]) +
    facet_wrap(~number, nrow = if (narrow) 3 else 1) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-0.4, 0.6, 0.2), labels = minus_labels(1),
                       limits = c(-0.32, 0.56), expand = expansion(0)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.7, top), expand = expansion(0)) +
    labs(x = 'Prose reply minus executed result (ms)', y = NULL) +
    theme_figure(base_size) +
    theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.spacing = unit(if (narrow) 0.9 else 1.4, 'lines'))
}
# The axis must hold every reply
stopifnot(range(unbalanced_prose_deviations) > -0.32, range(unbalanced_prose_deviations) < 0.56)

draw_narrow(fig_deviations(narrow = TRUE), width = 4.4, height = 5.2)
fig_deviations()
```

### What the Agents Chose When Left to Choose

Given the open request, the `r count_text(nrow(choices))` scripts converged on one analysis, a linear mixed-effects model of the untransformed reaction times with crossed random effects for participants and words. The maximal model, with by-participant and by-word priming slopes, gave a singular fit, one in which a random-effect variance is estimated at zero or a correlation at ±1. Its by-participant slope was perfectly correlated with the intercept, and every script dropped that slope. All `r count_text(nrow(choices))` then computed the interval from a *t* distribution with Satterthwaite's approximation of the degrees of freedom, which lmerTest adds to models fitted with lme4 [@kuznetsova2017]. `r stringr::str_to_sentence(count_text(sum(choices$frequency_covariate)))` also included word frequency as a covariate, although in a balanced design it cannot change the estimate, since every word appears after both types of prime.

Dropping that slope follows the parsimonious strategy of @matuschek2017 but sits uneasily with the maximal structure recommended by @barr2013. The sample suggested less variation across participants than across words, the reverse of the population pattern, so the agents faced the decision as an analyst would with real data, without the population values to go by.

The prose replies to the open request reached the same interval as the scripts by decomposing the `r count_text(nrow(paired))` paired differences into participant, word and residual components. In a balanced design, this decomposition gives the same standard error as the scripts' model without by-participant slopes. `r stringr::str_to_sentence(count_text(nrow(equated_maximal)))` of these replies equated their decomposition with the maximal model, although that model keeps a small by-participant slope and gives a slightly wider Satterthwaite interval, `r interval(maximal_ci[1], maximal_ci[2])` ms. With the specified request, both routes returned the Wald interval of the maximal model, which is narrower than either Satterthwaite interval because it takes its critical value from the normal distribution.

Every prose reply to the open request, and `r count_text(noted_by_route[['script']])` of the script summaries, also considered a paired *t* test over participants, whose interval, `r interval(paired_ci[1], paired_ci[2])` ms, excludes zero. They set it aside because it ignores the variation across words and so overstates the evidence for generalising beyond the words sampled. The effect is real here, so that test would have reached the right conclusion, but through an analysis too liberal for the purpose. The mixed-model intervals include zero, and they also contain the population effect of `r ms(population_effect, 1)` ms.

### Mixed Models by Hand

An agent that ran no code could still fit a mixed model, and the prose replies to the balanced data showed how. Because every participant saw every word after both types of prime, the restricted maximum likelihood (REML) fit of the mixed model reduces to a few mean squares and cross-products of the paired differences and of their sums. Cross-products are the counterparts of mean squares for covariances. Table 2 recomputes in R the intermediate quantities that recur across the replies. Where a reply does not state the residual mean square as R gives it, it rounds the value or gives the residual variance, which is half of it.

```{r}
library(lme4)

decomposition <- anova(lm(difference ~ participant + item, data = paired))
# The standard error of the model without by-participant slopes, from the mean
# square of the words
reduced_se <- sqrt(decomposition['item', 'Mean Sq'] / nrow(paired))
balanced$prime_c <- ifelse(balanced$prime == 'unrelated', 0.5, -0.5)
specified_fit <- lmer(rt ~ prime_c + (1 + prime_c | participant) + (1 + prime_c | item),
                      data = balanced)

comma <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ',', trim = TRUE)
quantities <- tibble::tribble(
  ~key, ~quantity, ~value,
  'sum', sprintf('Sum of the %s paired differences (ms)', comma(nrow(paired))), comma(sum(paired$difference)),
  'ms_participants', 'Mean square of the differences, participants', comma(decomposition['participant', 'Mean Sq']),
  'ms_items', 'Mean square of the differences, words', comma(decomposition['item', 'Mean Sq']),
  'ms_residual', 'Mean square of the differences, residual', comma(decomposition['Residuals', 'Mean Sq']),
  'se_reduced', 'Standard error without by-participant slopes (ms)', sprintf('%.2f', reduced_se),
  'se_specified', 'Standard error of the maximal model (ms)', sprintf('%.2f', sqrt(vcov(specified_fit)[2, 2])),
  'paired_interval', 'Paired *t* interval over participant means (ms)',
    sprintf('[%.1f, %.1f]', paired_ci[1], paired_ci[2])
)

# A reply states a value when every number in it appears in the reply with no
# digit or decimal point before it and no digit after it, ignoring thousands
# separators.
states <- function(value, texts) {
  numbers <- gsub(',', '', regmatches(value, gregexpr('[0-9][0-9,]*\\.?[0-9]*', value))[[1]])
  patterns <- sprintf('(?<![0-9.])%s(?![0-9])', gsub('.', '\\.', numbers, fixed = TRUE))
  texts <- gsub('(?<=[0-9]),(?=[0-9]{3})', '', texts, perl = TRUE)
  sum(Reduce(`&`, lapply(patterns, grepl, x = texts, perl = TRUE)))
}
prose_balanced <- runs$route == 'prose' & runs$data == 'balanced'
open_replies <- runs$reply[prose_balanced & runs$request == 'open']
specified_replies <- runs$reply[prose_balanced & runs$request == 'specified']
quantities$open <- vapply(quantities$value, states, integer(1), texts = open_replies)
quantities$specified <- vapply(quantities$value, states, integer(1), texts = specified_replies)

count_of <- function(k, n) sprintf('%d of %d', k, n)
knitr::kable(
  quantities |> transmute(Quantity = quantity, `Value in R` = value,
                          `Open request` = count_of(open, length(open_replies)),
                          `Specified request` = count_of(specified, length(specified_replies))),
  caption = paste(
    'Intermediate Quantities Recomputed in R and the Number of the First Round\'s Prose Replies to the',
    'Balanced Data Stating Each. Mean squares are in squared milliseconds. The last two columns count the replies to each request',
    'that state the value as R gives it, to the precision shown, with or without a thousands separator.'),
  align = c('l', 'r', 'r', 'r'))
```

```{r quantities-checks, include = FALSE}
# Every reply that does not state the residual mean square as R gives it
# rounds the value or gives the residual variance, half of it, as the text
# says: each reply names a value that is 41,0xx or 20,5xx. The pattern types
# those leading digits, so they are tied to the decomposition here.
residual_ms <- decomposition['Residuals', 'Mean Sq']
stopifnot(round(residual_ms, -2) == 41000, round(residual_ms / 2, -2) == 20500,
          all(grepl('41,?0[0-9]{2}|20,?5[0-9]{2}', c(open_replies, specified_replies))))
# How many replies to a request state a quantity, looked up by its key
replies_stating <- function(key, request) quantities[[request]][match(key, quantities$key)]
# The paired interval appears only in replies to the open request and the
# standard error of the maximal model only in replies to the specified one,
# as Table 2 shows
stopifnot(replies_stating('paired_interval', 'open') > 0, replies_stating('paired_interval', 'specified') == 0,
          replies_stating('se_specified', 'specified') > 0, replies_stating('se_specified', 'open') == 0)

# The by-participant slope and the correlation each reply to the specified
# request states, looked for after the words 'slope' and 'correlat', so that a
# standard error of 9.83 or a Wald interval written with a plus-minus sign
```
