```{r quantities-checks, include = FALSE}
# cannot stand in for them
slope_nine <- grepl('slope[^\n]{0,60}?(about|\u2248) ?(8\\.9|9) ms', specified_replies, perl = TRUE)
correlation_of_one <- function(sign) {
  grepl(sprintf('correlat[^\n]{0,40}?%s ?1(?![.,]?[0-9])', sign), specified_replies, perl = TRUE)
}
positive_one <- correlation_of_one('\\+')
either_sign_one <- correlation_of_one('\u00b1')
stopifnot(all(slope_nine), all(positive_one | either_sign_one),
          sum(!positive_one) == 1, sum(either_sign_one) == 1)

# The fit these replies reconstructed, and that the open-request scripts found
# singular: the by-participant slope sits at the boundary, perfectly correlated
# with the intercept
participant_effects <- VarCorr(specified_fit)$participant
participant_slope_sd <- attr(participant_effects, 'stddev')[['prime_c']]
stopifnot(isSingular(specified_fit),
          round(attr(participant_effects, 'correlation')[1, 2], 3) == 1,
          # 'about 9 ms', as the replies put it (slope_nine)
          round(participant_slope_sd) == 9)

# The decomposition of the paired differences gives the standard error of the
# model without by-participant slopes, as the text says, and the maximal model
# a larger one
reduced_fit <- lmer(rt ~ prime_c + (1 | participant) + (1 + prime_c | item), data = balanced)
# The two agree well within the second decimal, which Table 2 prints
stopifnot(abs(sqrt(vcov(reduced_fit)[2, 2]) - reduced_se) < 1e-3,
          sqrt(vcov(specified_fit)[2, 2]) > reduced_se)
```

From these quantities, every reply to the specified request recovered the main features of lme4's fit. Each found a by-participant slope with a standard deviation of about `r sprintf('%.0f', participant_slope_sd)` ms, whose correlation with the intercepts lay at the boundary (+1 in `r count_text(sum(positive_one))` replies and ±1 in the other).

### Where Hand Calculation Runs Out

Removing trials takes that shortcut away. Some participant-word pairs lose one observation or both, and the REML fit then has to be found iteratively. All `r count_text(runs_per_cell)` scripts estimated a priming effect of `r ms(unbalanced_script$estimate)` ms, which differs from the raw difference in means of `r ms(unbalanced_raw_difference)` ms. The specified Wald interval now excludes zero, with a lower bound of `r ms(unbalanced_script$lower)` ms, whereas with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, the same model's interval still includes it.

The prose replies worked from weighted per-word effects and from variances estimated from the observed mean squares. Each put the by-participant slope variance at or near zero, whereas the numerical fit kept that slope, with a standard deviation of `r ms(attr(unbalanced_participant, 'stddev')[['prime_c']], 1)` ms, perfectly correlated with the intercepts. The replies therefore lay closer to the model without that slope than to the executed result (Table 3).

```{r}
# unbalanced_script (the executed result, which every script printed) and
# unbalanced_prose (the prose replies, in launch order) are built with the
# hidden checks earlier on the page.
knitr::kable(
  bind_rows(
    unbalanced_script |> transmute(Source = sprintf('Executed scripts (all %d)', runs_per_cell), result_text),
    unbalanced_prose |> transmute(Source = sprintf('Prose reply %d', row_number()), result_text)
  ) |> rename(`Estimate [95% interval] (ms)` = result_text),
  caption = paste('Results for the Unbalanced Data in the First Round, as Each Run Wrote Them. The prose',
                  'replies are numbered',
                  'in launch order.'),
  align = c('l', 'r'))
```

The largest discrepancy in any reported number was only `r ms(max(largest_discrepancy), 2)` ms (Figure 1), and every prose reply called its numbers approximations, with a margin wider than its discrepancy. All their lower bounds, however, lay above the executed one, which was itself only `r ms(unbalanced_script$lower, 2)` ms above zero, close enough for the exact fit to decide whether the interval excluded zero.

### How Long Each Route Took

When the analysis was specified, code was by far the quicker route (Figure 2). The median script took `r sprintf('%.1f', specified_script_minutes)` minutes from request to final reply, against `r sprintf('%.1f', minutes_of(condition_levels[2], 'prose'))` for a prose reply on the balanced data and `r sprintf('%.1f', minutes_of(condition_levels[3], 'prose'))` on the unbalanced data. Once written, the scripts computed their result in `r sprintf('%.1f', max(specified_seconds))` seconds or less, R's start-up included.

Given the open request, the scripts took longer, since their agents compared models and ran checks, and their times overlapped those of the prose replies. The agents shared access to the model and ran in batches, so these durations include waiting as well as computation and are best read as orders of magnitude.

```{r minutes, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.6, fig.cap = cap_minutes, fig.alt = alt_minutes}
# A separate row for each route makes every median unambiguous, including in the open
# condition, where the two routes' durations overlap
fig_minutes <- function(narrow = FALSE, base_size = if (narrow) 12 else 11) {
  points <- runs |>
    group_by(condition, route_label) |> arrange(order, .by_group = TRUE) |>
    mutate(y = as.numeric(route_label) + seq(-0.15, 0.15, length.out = n())) |> ungroup()
  medians <- runs |>
    group_by(condition, route_label) |>
    summarise(minutes = median(minutes), .groups = 'drop') |>
    mutate(y = as.numeric(route_label), label = sprintf('%.1f', minutes))
  # The first median carries the word, so that the others can be read as numbers
  first <- which(medians$condition == condition_levels[1] & medians$route_label == route_levels[2])
  medians$label[first] <- paste('median', medians$label[first])
  ggplot(points, aes(minutes, y, colour = route_label, shape = route_label)) +
    geom_segment(aes(x = minutes, xend = minutes, y = y - 0.3, yend = y + 0.3), data = medians,
                 inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = fig_roles[['ink']], linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_point(size = 2.4) +
    geom_text(aes(minutes, y + 0.46, label = label), data = medians, inherit.aes = FALSE,
              colour = fig_roles[['ink']], size = label_size(base_size)) +
    facet_wrap(~condition, ncol = 1) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(fig_roles[c('prose', 'script')], route_levels)) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = setNames(c(16, 15), route_levels)) +
    scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 30), labels = c('0.5', '1', '2', '5', '10', '20', '30')) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:2, labels = c('Prose replies', 'Executed scripts'),
                       limits = c(0.6, 2.75), expand = expansion(0)) +
    labs(x = if (narrow) 'Minutes to final reply (log scale)'
             else 'Minutes from request to final reply (logarithmic scale)', y = NULL) +
    theme_figure(base_size) +
    theme(axis.text.y = element_text(colour = fig_roles[['ink']], size = rel(0.92)),
          panel.spacing = unit(0.6, 'lines'))
}
stopifnot(range(runs$minutes) > 0.5, range(runs$minutes) < 30)  # within the axis's labels

draw_narrow(fig_minutes(narrow = TRUE), width = 4.4, height = 5.8)
fig_minutes()
```

### A Second Round, at Medium Effort

```{r second-round, include = FALSE}
# The second round's runs (medium and xhigh, read with the first round's
# results before Table 1), with the condition, route, reply and text of each,
# as for the first round's (runs)
with_texts <- function(rows) {
  rows |>
    mutate(condition = runs$condition[match(run_id, runs$run_id)],
           route_label = runs$route_label[match(run_id, runs$run_id)],
           reply = mapply(second_text, round, run_id, 'response.txt', USE.NAMES = FALSE),
           text = mapply(function(rd, id, rte) second_text(rd, id, if (rte == 'script') 'analysis.R' else 'response.txt'),
                         round, run_id, route, USE.NAMES = FALSE))
}
medium_runs <- with_texts(medium)
xhigh_runs <- with_texts(xhigh)
cell_of <- function(rows, cond, rte) rows[rows$condition == cond & rows$route == rte, ]
# No text was repeated in either round, as the summary says
stopifnot(n_distinct(c(runs$text, medium_runs$text, xhigh_runs$text)) ==
            nrow(runs) + nrow(medium_runs) + nrow(xhigh_runs))

# Every script given the specified request returned the first round's numbers,
# which some wrote to four decimals
second_specified_scripts <- medium_runs[medium_runs$route == 'script' & medium_runs$request == 'specified', ]
same_numbers <- function(row, script) {
  all(round(round(c(row$estimate, row$lower, row$upper), 2) - c(script$estimate, script$lower, script$upper), 6) == 0)
}
four_decimals <- sum(decimals(vapply(second_specified_scripts$result_line, function(line) result_numbers(line)[1],
                                     character(1))) == 4)
stopifnot(vapply(seq_len(nrow(second_specified_scripts)), function(i)
            same_numbers(second_specified_scripts[i, ], first_of(second_specified_scripts$condition[i], 'script')), logical(1)),
          four_decimals > 0)

# Given the open request, each script either kept the by-word slope, with the
# first round's result, or dropped both slopes, with the Satterthwaite
# interval of the model with random intercepts only. None of the latter fitted
# the model with only the by-word slope (reduced_fit, fitted for Table 2's
# checks), which is not singular.
second_open_scripts <- cell_of(medium_runs, condition_levels[1], 'script')
intercepts_fit <- lmerTest::lmer(rt ~ prime_c + (1 | participant) + (1 | item), data = balanced)
intercepts_ci <- satterthwaite_ci(intercepts_fit)
kept_slope <- second_open_scripts$result_line == open_script$result_line
dropped_both <- vapply(second_open_scripts$result_line, function(line)
  all(result_numbers(line)[2:3] == sprintf('%.2f', intercepts_ci)), logical(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
by_word_sd <- attr(VarCorr(reduced_fit)$item, 'stddev')[['prime_c']]
dropped_texts <- second_open_scripts$text[dropped_both]
# The random-effects structures a script writes, each with its terms sorted,
# so that neither the order of the terms nor spacing matters
random_term <- '\\(1(\\+prime_c)?\\|\\|?(participant|item)\\)'
structures_in <- function(text) {
  compact <- gsub('[[:space:]]', '', text)
  found <- regmatches(compact, gregexpr(sprintf('%s(\\+%s)*', random_term, random_term), compact))[[1]]
  vapply(found, function(s) paste(sort(regmatches(s, gregexpr(random_term, s))[[1]]), collapse = '+'),
         character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
}
dropped_structures <- lapply(dropped_texts, structures_in)
# Every structure with a by-word slope in these scripts is the maximal one or
# the same without correlations, both of which each script fitted, and the
# fits of these and of the model with only the by-word slope put the standard
# deviation of that slope at the same whole number of milliseconds, which the
# discussion gives
with_word_slope <- vapply(c('(1 + prime_c | participant) + (1 + prime_c | item)',
                            '(1 + prime_c || participant) + (1 + prime_c || item)'),
                          structures_in, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
uncorrelated_fit <- lmer(rt ~ prime_c + (1 + prime_c || participant) + (1 + prime_c || item), data = balanced)
uncorrelated_sds <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(uncorrelated_fit))
uncorrelated_sds <- uncorrelated_sds[uncorrelated_sds$var1 %in% 'prime_c' & is.na(uncorrelated_sds$var2), ]
word_slope_sds <- c(maximal = sample_sds[['words']], reduced = by_word_sd,
                    uncorrelated = uncorrelated_sds$sdcor[startsWith(uncorrelated_sds$grp, 'item')])
stopifnot(all(kept_slope | dropped_both), any(kept_slope), any(dropped_both),
          intercepts_ci[1] > 0, open_script$lower < 0,
          # the discussion says that the interval contains the population effect
          intercepts_ci[1] < population_effect, population_effect < intercepts_ci[2],
          !isSingular(reduced_fit), n_distinct(round(word_slope_sds)) == 1, length(word_slope_sds) == 3,
          vapply(dropped_structures, function(found) {
            all(with_word_slope %in% found) && '(1|item)+(1|participant)' %in% found &&
              all(found[grepl('prime_c\\|\\|?item', found)] %in% with_word_slope)
          }, logical(1)),
          grepl('singular', second_open_scripts$reply[dropped_both], ignore.case = TRUE),
          # the summary and the abstract, which cannot run code, give these counts
          sum(dropped_both) == 5, nrow(second_open_scripts) == 8)
# The summaries of three of them stated that both slope variances were at or
# near zero, as the discussion says
zero_claims <- c(`2d6442b4` = 'because the slope variances were estimated at zero',
                 c8710529 = 'because the slope variances were estimated at zero',
                 `9d94880d` = 'essentially no variation in the priming effect across participants or items')
stopifnot(names(zero_claims) %in% second_open_scripts$run_id[dropped_both],
          mapply(grepl, zero_claims, second_open_scripts$reply[match(names(zero_claims), second_open_scripts$run_id)],
                 fixed = TRUE))
# A check on wording only: no other summary of these scripts uses 'zero' or 'no
# variation'. One of them says that the participant slope variance was
# estimated at exactly 0, which concerns one variance, not both, and passes
# only because it writes the digit.
stopifnot(!any(grepl('zero|no variation',
                     second_open_scripts$reply[dropped_both & !second_open_scripts$run_id %in% names(zero_claims)])))

# Every prose reply to the open request divided by the root of the number of
# participants, and all but one gave the by-participant paired interval. The
# other based a slightly different interval on the participants' means. Every
# reply of the first round had set that analysis aside, as the checks on
# noted_by_route and set_aside confirm.
second_open_prose <- cell_of(medium_runs, condition_levels[1], 'prose')
gave_paired <- vapply(second_open_prose$result_line, function(line)
  all(result_numbers(line)[2:3] == sprintf('%.1f', paired_ci)), logical(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
other_paired <- second_open_prose[!gave_paired, ]
stopifnot(all(grepl(paste0('√', spec_file$units$subject$n), second_open_prose$reply, fixed = TRUE)),
          sum(!gave_paired) == 1,
          grepl('based it on participant-level means', other_paired$reply, fixed = TRUE),
          other_paired$lower != round(paired_ci[1], 1))

# Given the specified request, the prose replies put the by-participant slope
# variance at or near zero. Most then gave about the Wald interval of the
# model without by-participant slopes, and the others, which also left out the
# by-word slope variance (in the phrases quoted), that of random intercepts only.
second_specified_prose <- cell_of(medium_runs, condition_levels[2], 'prose')
reduced_wald <- confint(reduced_fit, parm = 'prime_c', method = 'Wald')
intercepts_wald <- confint(intercepts_fit, parm = 'prime_c', method = 'Wald')
near_interval <- function(rows, target, tolerance) {
  abs(rows$lower - target[1]) <= tolerance & abs(rows$upper - target[2]) <= tolerance
}
# The tolerances admit the replies' rounding. Those near the first interval lie
# within 0.023 ms of its bounds, and the two near the second, written to one
# decimal, within 0.2 ms.
about_reduced <- near_interval(second_specified_prose, reduced_wald, 0.05)
about_intercepts <- near_interval(second_specified_prose, intercepts_wald, 0.25)
left_out <- c(`79c3e2a0` = 'I assumed the item slope variance is also small',
              b42ac192 = 'I did not compute the item slope variance')
stopifnot(all(about_reduced | about_intercepts), !any(about_reduced & about_intercepts),
          sum(about_reduced) > sum(about_intercepts),
          grepl('participant[^.]{0,120}(at|near|about) zero', second_specified_prose$reply),
          setequal(names(left_out), second_specified_prose$run_id[about_intercepts]),
          mapply(grepl, left_out, second_specified_prose$reply[match(names(left_out), second_specified_prose$run_id)],
                 fixed = TRUE))

# On the unbalanced data, the replies' estimates lie near the mean difference
# of the complete participant-word pairs, which each reply counted, and their
# lower bounds well above the executed one. The estimates lie within 0.5 ms of
# that mean, and the lowest lower bound 4.8 ms above the executed one.
second_unbalanced_prose <- cell_of(medium_runs, condition_levels[3], 'prose')
complete_pairs <- reshape(unbalanced[, c('participant', 'item', 'prime', 'rt')],
                          idvar = c('participant', 'item'), timevar = 'prime', direction = 'wide')
complete_pairs <- complete_pairs[complete.cases(complete_pairs), ]
complete_pair_mean <- mean(complete_pairs$rt.unrelated - complete_pairs$rt.related)
stopifnot(abs(second_unbalanced_prose$estimate - complete_pair_mean) < 0.6,
          second_unbalanced_prose$lower > unbalanced_script$lower + 4,
          grepl(nrow(complete_pairs), second_unbalanced_prose$reply, fixed = TRUE))

# No prose reply of the second round agreed, at its precision, with a script
# of either round in its condition, and none returned a result of the first
# round, as the summary, the abstract and the discussion say
second_prose <- medium_runs[medium_runs$route == 'prose', ]
scripts_both <- bind_rows(runs[runs$route == 'script', c('condition', 'estimate', 'lower', 'upper')],
                          medium_runs[medium_runs$route == 'script', c('condition', 'estimate', 'lower', 'upper')])
# As for the first round, rounding a script's number to the one or two
# decimals of a reply must not fall on a .5 boundary
script_numbers <- abs(unlist(scripts_both[c('estimate', 'lower', 'upper')]))
stopifnot(vapply(1:2, function(d) all(abs((script_numbers * 10^d) %% 1 - 0.5) > 1e-6), logical(1)))
matched_script <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(second_prose)), function(i) {
  candidates <- scripts_both[scripts_both$condition == second_prose$condition[i], ]
  any(vapply(seq_len(nrow(candidates)), function(j) agrees(second_prose[i, ], candidates[j, ]), logical(1)))
}, logical(1))
stopifnot(!any(matched_script), !(second_prose$result_line %in% runs$result_line[runs$route == 'prose']))

# The prose replies were faster in every condition than in the first round
prose_minutes <- function(rows) {
  prose <- rows[rows$route == 'prose', ]
  tapply(prose$minutes, droplevels(prose$condition), median)
}
first_prose_minutes <- prose_minutes(runs)
second_prose_minutes <- prose_minutes(medium_runs)
stopifnot(max(second_prose_minutes) < min(first_prose_minutes))

# The runs at xhigh returned the first round's results, which the same runs
# had not returned at medium effort, as the discussion says. The prose reply
# found lme4's boundary fit (a by-participant slope of about 9 ms, perfectly
# correlated with the intercepts), and the script kept the by-word slope.
xhigh_prose <- xhigh_runs[xhigh_runs$route == 'prose', ]
xhigh_script <- xhigh_runs[xhigh_runs$route == 'script', ]
minutes_from_seconds <- function(seconds) sprintf('%.1f', seconds / 60)
stopifnot(xhigh_runs$result_line == runs$result_line[match(xhigh_runs$run_id, runs$run_id)],
          medium_runs$result_line[match(xhigh_runs$run_id, medium_runs$run_id)] !=
            runs$result_line[match(xhigh_runs$run_id, runs$run_id)],
          grepl('slope SD comes out at about 9 ms, perfectly correlated', xhigh_prose$reply, fixed = TRUE),
          xhigh_script$result_line == open_script$result_line,
          xhigh_prose$thinking_seconds > max(second_specified_prose$thinking_seconds))

# Each script of the second round was executed twice, as the text says, and
# printed identical output both times, ending with the result line its agent
# reported
second_executions <- read.csv(file.path(experiment, 'rerun', 'executions.csv'),
                              colClasses = c(run_id = 'character'))
execution_key <- paste(second_executions$round, second_executions$run_id)
run_key <- paste(second$round, second$run_id)
stopifnot(setequal(execution_key, run_key[second$route == 'script']),
          all(table(execution_key) == 2), max(second_executions$execution) == 2,
          tapply(second_executions$stdout_sha256, execution_key, n_distinct) == 1,
          all(second_executions$status == 0),
          second_executions$result == second$result_line[match(execution_key, run_key)],
          n_distinct(second_executions$environment) == 1)

# No run of the second round given the specified request mentioned
# Satterthwaite or Kenward-Roger degrees of freedom, as the discussion says of
# both rounds
specified_both <- bind_rows(medium_runs, xhigh_runs) |> filter(request == 'specified')
stopifnot(!grepl('Satterthwaite|Kenward', c(specified_both$reply, specified_both$text), ignore.case = TRUE))

# The lengths of the scripts of both rounds, which the discussion gives
all_script_lines <- vapply(c(runs$text[runs$route == 'script'], medium_runs$text[medium_runs$route == 'script'],
                             xhigh_runs$text[xhigh_runs$route == 'script']),
                           function(text) length(strsplit(text, '\n')[[1]]), integer(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)

# The intervals on the balanced data that exclude zero in each round, which the text and
# Figure 3 give. The interval of the scripts with random intercepts only is among them,
# and shares its estimate with that of the scripts that kept the by-word slope, but is
# narrower, as the text says.
balanced_excluding <- c(first = sum(runs$data == 'balanced' & runs$lower > 0),
                        second = sum(medium_runs$data == 'balanced' & medium_runs$lower > 0))
stopifnot(balanced_excluding[['first']] == 0, balanced_excluding[['second']] > 0, intercepts_ci[1] > 0,
          n_distinct(round(second_open_scripts$estimate, 2)) == 1,
          diff(intercepts_ci) < open_script$upper - open_script$lower)
second_unbalanced_lower <- range(second_unbalanced_prose$lower)
cap_results <- sprintf(paste(
  'Every Result Reported in Either Round. Each line is one result, an estimate (marked) with its 95%% interval,',
  'rounded to two decimals, and the label beside it gives the number of runs that reported it, where more than',
  'one did. The dashed line marks zero and the dotted line the population effect. The first round ran at an',
  'unrecorded effort level, and the rounds also differed in date and software. The %s runs at xhigh effort are',
  'reported in the text.'), count_text(nrow(xhigh_runs)))
alt_results <- sprintf(paste(
  'Horizontal intervals in six panels, one for each condition in each round. In the first round, no interval on',
  'the balanced data excludes zero, and the prose replies to the unbalanced data lie within a fraction of a',
  'millisecond of the executed result. In the second round, %s of the %s intervals on the balanced data exclude',
  'zero, among them that of the %s open-request scripts that kept random intercepts only, and the prose replies',
  'to the unbalanced data have lower bounds of %s to %s ms, against %s ms for the scripts.'),
  balanced_excluding[['second']], sum(medium_runs$data == 'balanced'), count_text(sum(dropped_both)),
  sprintf('%.1f', second_unbalanced_lower[1]), sprintf('%.1f', second_unbalanced_lower[2]),
  sprintf('%.2f', unbalanced_script$lower))
```

Specifying the analysis kept the scripts on course. Given the specified request, all `r count_text(nrow(second_specified_scripts))` scripts of the second round returned the first round's results, `r count_text(four_decimals, nrow(second_specified_scripts))` of them to four decimals (Table 4). The open request split them. `r stringr::str_to_sentence(count_text(sum(kept_slope)))` scripts kept the by-word priming slope and returned the first round's interval, whereas `r count_text(sum(dropped_both))` dropped both random slopes after singular fits and kept random intercepts only. Their Satterthwaite interval, `r interval(intercepts_ci[1], intercepts_ci[2])` ms, excludes zero. None of those `r count_text(sum(dropped_both))` tried the model that drops only the by-participant slope. That model gives no singular fit, and lme4 puts the standard deviation of its by-word slope at `r ms(by_word_sd, 1)` ms, well away from the boundary.

```{r}
# runs holds the first round's runs and medium_runs the second's, built with
# the hidden checks above, and as_written() is defined before Table 1. A cell
# lists each result as the runs wrote it, with the number of runs that gave
# it, or, with more than max_listed results, the range of each of the three
# numbers. As in Table 1, the first round's replies to the unbalanced data,
# which gave several results, are left to Table 3. The result columns are
# left-aligned, unlike those of Tables 1 and 3, because their cells stack
# several results. Each result, and each range, is joined with non-breaking
# spaces, so that a line break can fall only between them.
max_listed <- 5
results_cell <- function(lines) {
  if (n_distinct(lines) > max_listed) {
    numbers <- t(vapply(lines, result_numbers, character(3), USE.NAMES = FALSE))
    span <- function(j) {
      value <- as.numeric(numbers[, j])
      sprintf('%s&nbsp;to&nbsp;%s', minus(numbers[which.min(value), j]), minus(numbers[which.max(value), j]))
    }
    return(sprintf('%s results, with estimates %s, lower bounds %s and upper bounds %s',
                   stringr::str_to_sentence(count_text(n_distinct(lines))), span(1), span(2), span(3)))
  }
  counts <- table(lines)
  lower <- as.numeric(vapply(names(counts), function(line) result_numbers(line)[2], character(1)))
  counts <- counts[order(-counts, lower)]
  paste(gsub(' ', '&nbsp;', sprintf('%s (%d)', as_written(names(counts)), as.vector(counts)), fixed = TRUE),
        collapse = '<br>')
}
by_cell <- function(rows) {
  rows |>
    group_by(condition, route_label) |>
    summarise(distinct = n_distinct(result_line), results = results_cell(result_line),
              minutes = sprintf('%.1f', median(minutes)), .groups = 'drop')
}
first_cells <- by_cell(runs) |> mutate(results = if_else(distinct == 1, results, 'See Table 3'))

# The stacked results would leave the first round's column too narrow for one
# interval, so this table's shares are fixed too (column_shares() is defined
# before Table 1). The headers break at a <br> and nowhere else, since the
# site keeps a header on one line, and the shares fit the table in the
# 720-pixel column of a desktop page.
column_shares(knitr::kable(
  inner_join(first_cells, by_cell(medium_runs), by = c('condition', 'route_label'),
             suffix = c('_first', '_second')) |>
    arrange(condition, desc(route_label)) |>
    select(condition, route_label, results_first, results_second, minutes_first, minutes_second),
  col.names = c('Condition', 'Route', 'Results,<br>first round', 'Results,<br>second round',
                'Minutes,<br>first round', 'Minutes,<br>second round'),
  caption = sprintf(paste(
    'Results and Times of the Runs in Each Condition and Route, by Round. The first round ran at the effort',
    'level of the session that launched it, and the second at medium effort. Each row covers %s runs in each',
    'round. A result is the estimate and 95%% interval in milliseconds as the runs wrote it, followed by the',
    'number of runs that gave it. Where a cell has more than %s results, the range of each number is',
    'given instead. Times are the median minutes from request to final reply. The %s runs at xhigh effort',
    'are reported in the text.'), count_text(runs_per_cell), count_text(max_listed), count_text(nrow(xhigh_runs))),
  align = c('l', 'l', 'l', 'l', 'r', 'r')), shares = c(17, 10, 23, 28, 11, 11))
```

None of the second round's prose replies reproduced a result of the first. All but one of the replies to the open request fell back on the by-participant paired interval, which every reply of the first round had set aside. Given the specified request on the balanced data, most approximated a model without by-participant slopes, and the others left out the by-word slope variance as well. On the unbalanced data, the replies put their estimates near the mean difference over complete participant-word pairs, with lower bounds well above the executed one (Table 4). They were also quicker in every condition than the replies of the first round.

Both runs repeated at xhigh effort returned the first round's results. The script kept the by-word slope, and the prose reply reconstructed lme4's boundary fit after `r minutes_from_seconds(xhigh_prose$thinking_seconds)` minutes of reasoning. Two runs cannot establish an effect of the effort level, but they show that the answers at medium effort were not the only ones this model would give.

Figure 3 sets every result of both rounds side by side. Each condition came with the same data in both rounds, yet on the balanced data, no interval of the first round excluded zero, whereas `r count_text(balanced_excluding[['second']], sum(medium_runs$data == 'balanced'))` of the `r count_text(sum(medium_runs$data == 'balanced'))` intervals of the second round did. Among them is the interval of the `r count_text(sum(dropped_both))` scripts that kept random intercepts only, which shares its estimate with that of the scripts that kept the by-word slope but is narrower.

```{r all-results, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6.2, fig.cap = cap_results, fig.alt = alt_results}
# runs holds the first round's runs and medium_runs the second's. Each line is one
# distinct result in a condition and route, with the number of runs that reported it.
# Some scripts of the second round wrote four decimals, which round to the first
# round's numbers, so the results are compared at two decimals, as the tables show them.
round_names <- c('First round', 'Second round, medium effort')
results_both <- bind_rows(runs |> mutate(round = round_names[1]),
                          medium_runs |> mutate(round = round_names[2])) |>
  mutate(across(c(estimate, lower, upper), \(x) round(x, 2)),
         round = factor(round, levels = round_names)) |>
  count(round, condition, route_label, estimate, lower, upper, name = 'runs') |>
  group_by(round, condition) |>
  # the scripts' results above the replies', each set from the lowest lower bound
  arrange(desc(route_label), lower, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(slot = row_number() + 0.5 * (route_label == route_levels[1])) |>
  ungroup()
stopifnot(sum(results_both$runs) == nrow(runs) + nrow(medium_runs))

# The two models of the second round's open-request scripts, named beside their counts
open_two <- results_both$round == round_names[2] & results_both$condition == condition_levels[1] &
  results_both$route_label == route_levels[2]
model_name <- ifelse(results_both$lower == round(intercepts_ci[1], 2), 'random intercepts only',
                     ifelse(results_both$lower == open_script$lower, 'by-word slope kept', NA))
stopifnot(sum(open_two) == 2, !anyNA(model_name[open_two]),
          results_both$runs[open_two] == c(sum(kept_slope), sum(dropped_both))[match(model_name[open_two],
            c('by-word slope kept', 'random intercepts only'))])
results_both$label <- ifelse(open_two, sprintf('×%d, %s', results_both$runs, model_name),
                             ifelse(results_both$runs > 1, sprintf('×%d', results_both$runs), ''))

fig_results <- function(narrow = FALSE, base_size = if (narrow) 12 else 11) {
  lines <- results_both |> mutate(y = -slot)
  if (narrow) {
    lines$panel <- factor(paste(lines$condition, tolower(lines$round), sep = ', '),
                          levels = as.vector(t(outer(condition_levels, tolower(round_names), paste, sep = ', '))))
  }
  # The population effect is named once, above the first panel, which gets room for it
  first <- lines$condition == condition_levels[1] & lines$round == round_names[1]
  truth <- lines[first, ][1, ] |>
    mutate(x = population_effect + 1, y = if (narrow) 1.05 else 0.25,
           label = sprintf('Population effect, %s ms', sprintf('%.1f', population_effect)))
  room <- lines[first, ][1, ] |> mutate(y = if (narrow) 1.7 else 0.9)
  route_names <- c('Executed scripts', 'Prose replies')
  plot <- ggplot(lines, aes(y = y, colour = route_label, shape = route_label)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = fig_roles[['rule']], linewidth = 0.5, linetype = 'dashed') +
    geom_vline(xintercept = population_effect, colour = fig_roles[['ink']], linewidth = 0.5, linetype = 'dotted') +
    geom_segment(aes(x = lower, xend = upper, yend = y), linewidth = 1.1, lineend = 'butt') +
    geom_point(aes(x = estimate), size = 2.3) +
    geom_text(aes(x = upper + 1.2, label = label), hjust = 0, colour = fig_roles[['muted']],
              size = 0.9 * label_size(base_size), show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_text(aes(x = x, y = y, label = label), data = truth, inherit.aes = FALSE, hjust = 0, vjust = 0,
              colour = fig_roles[['ink']], size = 0.9 * label_size(base_size)) +
    geom_blank(aes(x = population_effect, y = y), data = room, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(fig_roles[c('prose', 'script')], route_levels),
                        breaks = rev(route_levels), labels = route_names, name = NULL) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = setNames(c(16, 15), route_levels),
                       breaks = rev(route_levels), labels = route_names, name = NULL) +
    # Labels that run past the last panel draw into the margin kept for them
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-4, if (narrow) 64 else 50), clip = 'off') +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 40, 10), expand = expansion(0)) +
    labs(x = 'Reported estimate and 95% interval (ms)', y = NULL) +
    theme_figure(base_size) +
    theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), legend.position = 'top', legend.justification = 'left',
          legend.location = 'plot', legend.text = element_text(colour = fig_roles[['ink']], size = rel(0.92)),
          legend.margin = margin(0, 0, 4, 0), legend.key.spacing.x = unit(14, 'pt'))
  if (narrow) {
    plot + facet_grid(panel ~ ., scales = 'free_y', space = 'free_y') +
      geom_text(aes(x = -4, y = 0.25, label = panel), data = distinct(lines, panel), inherit.aes = FALSE,
                hjust = 0, vjust = 0, fontface = 'bold', colour = fig_roles[['ink']],
                size = 0.95 * label_size(base_size)) +
      scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(add = c(0.7, 0.95))) +
      theme(strip.text.y = element_blank(), panel.spacing = unit(0.3, 'lines'))
  } else {
    plot + facet_grid(condition ~ round, scales = 'free_y', space = 'free_y', switch = 'y',
                      labeller = labeller(condition = label_wrap_gen(17))) +
      scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(add = 0.7)) +
      theme(strip.placement = 'outside',
            strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0, vjust = 1, face = 'bold',
                                             colour = fig_roles[['ink']], size = rel(0.92)),
            panel.spacing.x = unit(1.2, 'lines'), panel.spacing.y = unit(0.8, 'lines'),
            plot.margin = margin(6, 92, 6, 6))
  }
}
stopifnot(min(results_both$lower) > -4, max(results_both$upper) < 50)  # within the axis

draw_narrow(fig_results(narrow = TRUE), width = 4.4, height = 10.5)
fig_results()
```

### Executing the Scripts Again

Executing a script again in the same environment tests whether it is repeatable, and executing it elsewhere tests whether it travels. Every execution below used a fresh R process in the C locale, a standard set of language and character conventions. Checksums compared the output line by line, allowing for the different line endings of Windows and Linux. The scripts use `r knitr::combine_words(packages_loaded, and = ' and ', oxford_comma = FALSE)`, and some also call pbkrtest for the Kenward–Roger method, which adjusts the standard error as well as the degrees of freedom.

```{r environment-record, include = FALSE}
scripts <- design |> filter(route == 'script')
n_scripts <- nrow(scripts)
stored <- executions |> filter(execution == 1)
stored_of <- function(run_id, column) stored[[column]][match(run_id, stored$run_id)]

# The versions an environment string records. packageVersion() writes a CRAN
# version such as 1.1-35.1 as 1.1.35.1, so the hyphen is restored.
cran <- function(version) sub('^([0-9]+\\.[0-9]+)\\.', '\\1-', version)
versions_of <- function(environment) {
  stopifnot(length(environment) == 1)  # one environment per record, so [[1]] cannot drop one
  parts <- regmatches(environment, regexec(
    '^R ([^ ]+) \\(([^,]+), [^)]*\\) with lme4 ([^,]+), lmerTest ([^ ]+) and Matrix (.+)$',
    environment))[[1]]
  data.frame(System = if (grepl('linux', parts[3])) 'Linux' else if (grepl('mingw', parts[3])) 'Windows'
                      else if (grepl('darwin', parts[3])) 'macOS' else parts[3],
             R = parts[2], lme4 = cran(parts[4]), lmerTest = cran(parts[5]), Matrix = cran(parts[6]))
}
# running_under() comes from the hidden chunk on the second round's design
stored_versions <- versions_of(unique(stored$environment))
stored_system <- running_under('executions_session_info.txt')
# The versions under which the second round's scripts were executed, which
# differ in R and lme4 from those of the first round, as the Limits say
second_versions <- versions_of(unique(second_executions$environment))
stopifnot(second_versions$R != stored_versions$R, second_versions$lme4 != stored_versions$lme4)
stored_release <- sub('^(Ubuntu [0-9]+\\.[0-9]+).*$', '\\1', stored_system)

# The stored environment rebuilt from its record by the Dockerfile, where
# verify_executions.R executed every script on GitHub Actions and listed the
# versions of the Ubuntu packages
verification <- read.csv(file.path(experiment, 'verification.csv'), colClasses = c(run_id = 'character'))
rebuild_record <- readLines(file.path(experiment, 'verification_session_info.txt'))
rebuild_release <- sub('^(Ubuntu [0-9]+\\.[0-9]+).*$', '\\1', running_under('verification_session_info.txt'))
rebuild_version <- function(package) {
  listed <- grep(sprintf('^r-cran-%s ', tolower(package)), rebuild_record, value = TRUE)
  sub('\\+.*$', '', sub('-[^-]+$', '', sub('^\\S+ ', '', listed)))
}

# The check on one machine with three package libraries that differ only in
# the versions of lme4 and lmerTest (check_versions.R), keeping the last
# attempt at each script
version_check <- read.csv(file.path(experiment, 'version_check.csv'), colClasses = c(run_id = 'character'))
checked <- version_check |>
  group_by(library, run_id) |> filter(attempt == max(attempt)) |> ungroup() |>
  mutate(same_output = status == 0 & stdout_sha256 == stored_of(run_id, 'stdout_sha256'),
         same_result = status == 0 & result == stored_of(run_id, 'result'))
library_rows <- function(library) checked[checked$library == library, ]
library_versions <- function(library) versions_of(unique(library_rows(library)$environment))
newer_versions <- library_versions('renv.lock')
newer_system <- sub('^(Windows [0-9]+).*$', '\\1', running_under('version_check_session_info.txt'))

# The versions of the other packages the scripts load, in the rebuild and in the
# library with the earlier lme4, and those that differ
package_version_in <- function(package, library) {
  listed <- unique(library_rows(library)$packages)
  sub(sprintf('^(.*, )?%s ([^,]+).*$', package), '\\2', listed)
}
# Typed so as to set the order of the list in the text, and checked against the
# packages the scripts load, with pbkrtest, which lmerTest calls
other_packages <- c('emmeans', 'pbkrtest', 'dplyr', 'tidyr')
stopifnot(setequal(other_packages, setdiff(c(packages_loaded, 'pbkrtest'), c('lme4', 'lmerTest', 'Matrix'))))
other_changed <- other_packages[vapply(other_packages, function(p)
  numeric_version(rebuild_version(p)) != numeric_version(package_version_in(p, 'lme4 1.1-35.1')),
  logical(1))]

# The two also differed in their linear-algebra libraries and in packages that
# lme4 depends on, such as nloptr, which the library with the earlier lme4 took
# from renv.lock. The records write LAPACK's version in different forms on
# Linux and Windows, so only the version number is compared. (A system LAPACK
# and R's own differ even at the same version, so this is the strictest check
# available, not the only evidence.)
lock <- jsonlite::read_json(lock_file)
lapack_of <- function(file) {
  line <- grep('LAPACK', readLines(file.path(experiment, file)), value = TRUE)[1]
  version <- regmatches(line, regexpr('[0-9]+(\\.[0-9]+)+', line))
  # Without a dotted version, the comparison below would pass on an empty value
  stopifnot(length(version) == 1)
  version
}
stopifnot(vapply(c('nloptr', 'minqa', 'Rcpp', 'RcppEigen'), function(p)
            numeric_version(rebuild_version(p)) != numeric_version(lock$Packages[[p]]$Version), logical(1)),
          lapack_of('verification_session_info.txt') != lapack_of('version_check_session_info.txt'))

# What the newer lme4 changed, from the kept outputs of the two libraries that
# differ only in its version. A printed table of random effects runs from its
# 'Groups' header to its 'Residual' row, and a likelihood-ratio table from its
# header to the next blank line.
read_output <- function(folder, id) {
  readLines(file.path(experiment, 'outputs', folder, paste0(id, '.txt')), warn = FALSE)
}
# The scripts that report Kenward-Roger degrees of freedom, counted in the text
# from their code, are those whose stored output mentions them
stopifnot(kenward_scripts == sum(vapply(scripts$run_id, function(id)
  any(grepl('Kenward', read_output('stored-lme4', id))), logical(1))))
numbers_in <- function(lines) sort(unlist(regmatches(lines, gregexpr('-?[0-9]+(\\.[0-9]+)?', lines))))
trailing_spaces <- function(lines) nchar(lines) - nchar(sub(' +$', '', lines))
changes <- bind_rows(lapply(scripts$run_id, function(id) {
  earlier <- read_output('stored-lme4', id)
  newer <- read_output('renv-lock', id)
  stopifnot(length(earlier) == length(newer))
  residual_rows <- grep('^ Residual ', newer)
  tables <- lapply(grep('^ Groups ', newer), function(start)
    start:min(residual_rows[residual_rows >= start]))
  correlated <- vapply(tables, function(rows) grepl('Corr', newer[rows[1]]), logical(1))
  renamed <- grep('-2*log(L)', newer, fixed = TRUE)
  renamed <- renamed[grepl('deviance', earlier[renamed])]
  blank <- which(trimws(newer) == '')
  ratio_tables <- unlist(lapply(renamed, function(start) start:(min(blank[blank > start]) - 1)))
  data.frame(
    run_id = id,
    correlated_tables = sum(correlated),
    one_more_space = all(vapply(tables[correlated], function(rows)
      all(trailing_spaces(newer[rows]) == trailing_spaces(earlier[rows]) + 1), logical(1))),
    uncorrelated_unchanged = all(vapply(tables[!correlated], function(rows)
      all(earlier[rows] == newer[rows]), logical(1))),
    reordered = sum(vapply(tables[correlated], function(rows)
      grepl('Std.Dev. Variance', earlier[rows[1]], fixed = TRUE) &&
        grepl('Variance +Std.Dev.', newer[rows[1]]), logical(1))),
    renamed = length(renamed),
    # every changed line lies in one of those tables
    explained = all(which(earlier != newer) %in% c(unlist(tables[correlated]), ratio_tables)),
    same_numbers = identical(numbers_in(earlier), numbers_in(sub('-2*log(L)', 'deviance', newer, fixed = TRUE))))
}))

# The claims of this section, of the discussion and of the summary and the
# abstract rest on these
libraries <- c('renv.lock', 'lme4 1.1-35.1', 'lme4 1.1-35.1 and lmerTest 3.1-3')
earlier_lme4 <- library_versions('lme4 1.1-35.1')
stopifnot(
  # the records are complete
  setequal(verification$run_id, scripts$run_id), setequal(unique(checked$library), libraries),
  all(table(checked$library)[libraries] == n_scripts),
  # each script ran once in the rebuild and in each library, as Table 5 says
  nrow(verification) == n_scripts, all(version_check$attempt == 1),
  # the rebuild matches the stored environment and reproduced its output
  unique(verification$environment) == unique(stored$environment), rebuild_release == stored_release,
  all(verification$identical),
  # the libraries differ only in lme4 and lmerTest, as the text says
  n_distinct(gsub('(lme4|lmerTest) [^,]+, ', '', version_check$packages)) == 1,
  earlier_lme4$lme4 == stored_versions$lme4, earlier_lme4$lmerTest == newer_versions$lmerTest,
  library_versions(libraries[3])$lmerTest == stored_versions$lmerTest,
  n_distinct(vapply(libraries, function(l) library_versions(l)$Matrix, character(1))) == 1,
  # with the earlier lme4 the output is the stored one, and with the newer lme4
  # only its formatting differs
  all(library_rows(libraries[2])$same_output), all(library_rows(libraries[3])$same_output),
  !any(library_rows('renv.lock')$same_output), all(library_rows('renv.lock')$same_result),
  all(changes$correlated_tables > 0), all(changes$one_more_space), all(changes$uncorrelated_unchanged),
  all(changes$explained), all(changes$same_numbers), any(changes$renamed > 0), any(changes$reordered > 0),
  # and the rest of the environment differed
  earlier_lme4$System != stored_versions$System, earlier_lme4$R != stored_versions$R,
  earlier_lme4$Matrix != stored_versions$Matrix, earlier_lme4$lmerTest != stored_versions$lmerTest,
  length(other_changed) > 0,
  numeric_version(newer_versions$lme4) > numeric_version(stored_versions$lme4))
```

The first round's `r count_text(nrow(executions))` stored executions used R `r stored_versions$R` on `r sub(' LTS$', '', stored_system)`, with lme4 `r stored_versions$lme4`, lmerTest `r stored_versions$lmerTest` and Matrix `r stored_versions$Matrix`, and every script printed identical output each time. A [Dockerfile](`r experiment_url('Dockerfile')`) rebuilds that environment from a dated snapshot of the software, and on a fresh machine on GitHub, all `r count_text(nrow(verification))` scripts reproduced their stored output, as [verification.csv](`r experiment_url('verification.csv')`) records.

The second round's `r count_text(n_distinct(execution_key))` scripts were each executed twice in the library their agents had used, under R `r second_versions$R` on `r second_versions$System`. They too printed identical output, ending with the result each agent had reported.

```{r rerun}
# run_script_with_retries(), data_file_for() and child_environment() come from
# experiment/run_script.R. The list of scripts (scripts, n_scripts) and their
# stored executions (stored_of()) are read from design.csv and executions.csv
# earlier on the page.
source(file.path(experiment, 'run_script.R'))

# Every script executed once more, and again if its R process crashes, which
# happens occasionally on Windows
rerun_attempts <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(n_scripts), function(i)
  run_script_with_retries(scripts$run_id[i], data_file_for(scripts$data[i]),
                          experiment_dir = normalizePath(experiment), label = 'page')))
rerun <- rerun_attempts |> group_by(run_id) |> filter(attempt == max(attempt)) |> ungroup()
rerun <- rerun[match(scripts$run_id, rerun$run_id), ]
page_environment <- child_environment()

# Rscript exits with status 1 when a script stops with an error. Any other
# nonzero status means that the R process itself ended abnormally, as when it
# crashes, which says nothing about the script.
rerun$outcome <- ifelse(rerun$status == 0, 'completed', ifelse(rerun$status == 1, 'error', 'crash'))
rerun$same_result <- rerun$outcome == 'completed' & !is.na(rerun$result) &
  rerun$result == stored_of(rerun$run_id, 'result')
rerun$same_output <- rerun$outcome == 'completed' &
  rerun$stdout_sha256 == stored_of(rerun$run_id, 'stdout_sha256')

c(stored_executions = nrow(executions), scripts = n_scripts,
  completed_now = sum(rerun$outcome == 'completed'),
  completed_after_a_crash = sum(rerun$outcome == 'completed' & rerun$attempt > 1),
  stopped_with_error_now = sum(rerun$outcome == 'error'), crashed_now = sum(rerun$outcome == 'crash'),
  same_result_now = sum(rerun$same_result), same_output_now = sum(rerun$same_output))
```

```{r rerun-text, include = FALSE}
# The wording of the paragraph below, from the counts above
n_completed <- sum(rerun$outcome == 'completed')
n_error <- sum(rerun$outcome == 'error')
n_crash <- sum(rerun$outcome == 'crash')
n_retried <- sum(rerun$outcome == 'completed' & rerun$attempt > 1)
n_same_result <- sum(rerun$same_result)
n_same_output <- sum(rerun$same_output)
# The abstract says that under newer versions the output changed only in its
# formatting, so every execution that completes must print the stored result
# line, whatever its output otherwise
stopifnot(n_same_result == n_completed)

# How a crashed process ended. Windows reports an access violation as status
# -1073741819 (0xC0000005), and processx reports a Unix signal as its negative.
crash_kind <- function(status) {
  if (status == -1073741819) 'an access violation'
  else if (.Platform$OS.type == 'unix' && status < 0) sprintf('signal %d', -status)
  else sprintf('exit status %d', status)
}
crash_kinds <- knitr::combine_words(unique(vapply(rerun$status[rerun$outcome == 'crash'],
                                                  crash_kind, character(1))), and = ' or ')

completed_text <- if (n_completed == n_scripts) {
  sprintf('All %s scripts ran to completion', count_text(n_scripts))
} else {
  sprintf('Of the %s scripts, %s ran to completion', count_text(n_scripts), count_text(n_completed, n_scripts))
}
rerun_text <- if (n_same_output == n_scripts) {
  sprintf('All %s scripts printed the same output as the stored executions.', count_text(n_scripts))
} else if (n_completed == 0) {
  sprintf('None of the %s scripts ran to completion.', count_text(n_scripts))
} else if (n_same_output == n_completed) {
  sprintf('%s and printed the same output as the stored executions.', completed_text)
} else {
  sprintf('%s and printed the same result line as the stored executions, but %s printed identical output.',
          completed_text, if (n_same_output == 0) 'none' else sprintf('only %s', count_text(n_same_output, n_scripts)))
}
retry_text <- if (n_retried == 0) '' else {
  sprintf(' In %s of them, the R process crashed at first and the script completed when executed again.',
          count_text(n_retried, n_scripts))
}
# The scripts that did not complete are 'the other' ones only if some did
failure_text <- if (n_error + n_crash == 0) {
  ''
} else if (n_completed == 0 && n_crash == 0) {
  ' All of them stopped with an error.'
} else if (n_completed == 0 && n_error == 0) {
  sprintf(' In all of them, the R process itself crashed with %s on every attempt.', crash_kinds)
} else if (n_completed == 0) {
  sprintf(' Of these, %s stopped with an error, and in %s the R process itself crashed with %s on every attempt.',
          count_text(n_error), count_text(n_crash), crash_kinds)
} else if (n_crash == 0) {
  sprintf(' The other %s stopped with an error.', count_text(n_error))
} else if (n_error == 0) {
  sprintf(' In the other %s, the R process itself crashed with %s on every attempt.', count_text(n_crash), crash_kinds)
} else {
  sprintf(' Of the other %s, %s stopped with an error, and in %s the R process itself crashed with %s on every attempt.',
          count_text(n_error + n_crash), count_text(n_error), count_text(n_crash), crash_kinds)
}

# The page is knitted with the version of R and the packages that renv.lock
# (read above) pins, and the text calls them newer than those of the stored
# executions
page_versions <- versions_of(page_environment)
version_columns <- c('R', 'lme4', 'lmerTest', 'Matrix')
stopifnot(page_versions$R == lock$R$Version,
          vapply(c('lme4', 'lmerTest', 'Matrix'), function(p)
            page_versions[[p]] == lock$Packages[[p]]$Version, logical(1)),
          numeric_version(page_versions$R) > numeric_version(stored_versions$R),
          numeric_version(page_versions$lme4) > numeric_version(stored_versions$lme4),
          # the page runs in the library that check_versions.R recorded as
          # renv.lock, as the text and Table 5 say
          unlist(page_versions[version_columns]) == unlist(newer_versions[version_columns]))
```

This page executes each of the first round's scripts once more whenever it is knitted, under the versions of R and its packages recorded in the site's lockfile, [renv.lock](`r sprintf('%s/blob/%s/renv.lock', repo_url, last_commit(lock_file))`), which are newer than the first round's. `r rerun_text``r retry_text``r failure_text`

To find the source of the difference, I also executed each script on one `r newer_system` machine with three libraries that differed only in their versions of lme4 and lmerTest (Table 5). Matrix stayed at `r newer_versions$Matrix` in all three, since the stored version could not be installed under the newer R. With the earlier lme4, both versions of lmerTest reproduced the stored output, as the Docker rebuild had. The newer lme4 changed only the formatting. It added a trailing space to the lines of some random-effects tables, renamed a column from `deviance` to `-2*log(L)` and, in some tables, swapped the columns of variances and standard deviations. None of the numbers changed.

```{r environments}
labels <- c(`renv.lock` = 'Newer (renv.lock)', `lme4 1.1-35.1` = 'Newer, with lme4 as stored',
            `lme4 1.1-35.1 and lmerTest 3.1-3` = 'Newer, with lme4 and lmerTest as stored')
# count_of() writes 'k of n', as in Table 2
row_of <- function(label, system, versions, same_output, same_result) {
  data.frame(Environment = label, `Operating system` = system, versions[, c('R', 'lme4', 'lmerTest', 'Matrix')],
             `Identical output` = count_of(sum(same_output), length(same_output)),
             `Same result line` = count_of(sum(same_result), length(same_result)), check.names = FALSE)
}
environment_table <- bind_rows(
  row_of('Stored, rebuilt with Docker', rebuild_release, versions_of(unique(verification$environment)),
         verification$identical, verification$result == stored_of(verification$run_id, 'result')),
  bind_rows(lapply(names(labels), function(library) {
    rows <- library_rows(library)
    row_of(labels[[library]], newer_system, library_versions(library), rows$same_output, rows$same_result)
  })))

knitr::kable(environment_table,
  caption = sprintf(paste(
    'Output of the First Round\'s Scripts in %s Environments, Compared With Their Stored Executions.',
    'Each script was executed once in each environment. \'Identical output\' counts the scripts whose',
    'output matched the stored output line for line, and \'Same result line\' counts those whose result',
    'line matched.'),
    stringr::str_to_title(count_text(nrow(environment_table)))),
  align = c('l', 'l', 'r', 'r', 'r', 'r', 'r', 'r'))
```

### What These Runs Can Establish

The experiment used one language model and one simulated data set, clean and fully described in the prompt, on which the lower bound of the interval lay close to zero. Real data bring exclusions, coding errors and gaps in documentation that these agents never faced. I designed the follow-up after seeing the results on the balanced data. The specified request also supplied the model formula and the function for the interval, so the agreement among its scripts tested implementation more than analysis. The prose route imitated a chat without a code interpreter, although many chat assistants now have one. An assistant that runs code and lets the researcher keep it could close much of the gap with a coding agent.

The two rounds differed in date, in the version of Claude Code, in the operating system and in the versions of R and lme4 that the agents worked with. The first round's effort level, that of the session that launched it, went unrecorded, and only two runs were repeated at xhigh. The differences between the rounds therefore cannot be put down to the effort level alone. With `r count_text(runs_per_cell)` runs in each combination of condition and route, the counts describe these runs and do not estimate error rates. Finally, I wrote every prompt as someone who reads R, so the experiment cannot show what a researcher without R would achieve with the same agents.

## Discussion

### What Executing the Code Added

No text in this experiment was repeated, yet every executed script printed the same output each time it ran. Because the versions of R, lme4, lmerTest and Matrix were recorded and can still be installed, the first round's scripts printed that output on another machine too. Under newer versions, their output changed only in its formatting. The scripts also left a record of the calculation that no prose reply could supply. Even where a reply matched the scripts, only recomputing its quantities could tell a correct reply from a confident error.

A reproducible analysis can still be a poor one, however [@leek2015]. The `r count_text(sum(dropped_both))` scripts of the second round that dropped both random slopes printed identical output each time they ran. Their interval excludes zero and points the right way, because the effect is real in this simulation. With real data, nobody could know that. Leaving out a by-word slope when the effect varies across words makes a test too liberal [@barr2013], so the same analysis would claim an effect more readily where none existed.

Agreement between runs is a separate matter. Many-analysts studies, which give one data set and one question to many teams, find wide variation among human analysts [@silberzahn2018; @breznau2022]. Autonomous AI analysts given one data set and one hypothesis also reached divergent verdicts that shifted with the language model and the prompt [@bertran2026]. @alizadeh2026 ran Claude Code and Codex 20 times each on one of those many-analysts studies [@breznau2022]. The agents varied their model specifications at least as much as the human teams had, yet their estimates stayed broadly in line with the human consensus. The authors located the agents' vulnerability in interpretation more than in estimation.

The task in this experiment was far simpler, and the close agreement of the first round may reflect a shared preference as much as independent confirmation, since runs of one model are not independent analysts. When @herdagdelen2026 left Claude Opus 4.8 to make the five decisions of an analysis with no preference assigned to it, it made the same five choices in 112 of 123 runs. Forty-eight runs of one model that agree may amount to one opinion stated 48 times.

@bertran2026 propose giving AI analysts a published specification, to reveal how much of their disagreement comes from underspecified choices. Here, the specified request kept the scripts consistent across rounds, whereas the open request divided them over one random slope, which decided whether their interval excluded zero. That consistency belonged to one model, at one effort level, on one structured task, and it may not survive the model's next update [@chen2024]. What can be kept is the code and a record of its environment, and together they leave any such difference open to inspection.

### Where Coding Literacy Comes In

By coding literacy, I mean being able to read and write code well enough to tell what a script does. The experiment did not vary it, but it shows where literacy came into the work, and at those points, much of what was needed turned out to be statistical knowledge.

Writing the specified request required knowing that the data call for crossed random effects, that the choice of random slopes changes the interval [@barr2013] and that transforming reaction times can change the effects being tested [@lo2015]. Coding came in only where the request named the function that fits the model, wrote the model in lme4's formula notation and gave the call to `confint()` that computes the interval. I cannot say how much that helped, since no condition stated the same analysis in plain statistical language.

The same request shows the limits of a specification. It fixed a Wald interval, which can be too narrow with few participants or items [@luke2017], and I chose it because one function call defines it exactly and so makes the scripts comparable. On the unbalanced data, that choice decided whether the interval excluded zero. An analysis for publication should use Satterthwaite or Kenward–Roger degrees of freedom, as the open-request scripts did, yet none of the `r count_text(nrow(specified_runs) + nrow(specified_both))` runs given the specified request, in either round, mentioned either. On this point, the agents left to choose did better than my specification.

Reading the code is the second point of entry. The scripts were only `r min(all_script_lines)` to `r max(all_script_lines)` lines long, short enough for a researcher who reads R to confirm in a few minutes that each fits the intended model to the intended rows. In the second round, the summaries of `r count_text(length(zero_claims))` of the `r count_text(sum(dropped_both))` scripts that dropped both slopes justified doing so by calling their variances zero or nearly so. A reader of R would notice that none of these scripts tried the model that drops only the by-participant slope. Printing the fits they discarded would also show that every model with the by-word slope put its standard deviation at about `r sprintf('%.0f', word_slope_sds[['uncorrelated']])` ms. Without that reading, the researcher is left with the agent's summary of its own work, which is more text from the same language model. Even so, what a reader would catch here is a statistical choice written in code, since no result pointed to a coding bug.

A reader of R is not the only possible remedy. Given the open request at xhigh effort, the one script I ran kept the by-word slope with nobody reading it. `r stringr::str_to_sentence(count_text(sum(kept_slope)))` of the `r count_text(nrow(second_open_scripts))` at medium effort did too, however, so this is only a hint that a setting may do part of a reader's work. A second agent asked to review each script might do more, although runs of one model may share its preferences, and different models often err in the same way [@kim2025]. The experiment did not test this.

Studies of how people use these tools complicate the picture. Anthropic, the maker of Claude Code, analysed about 400,000 sessions with it and concluded that the ability to steer the agent comes more from command of a domain than from the ability to write code [@hitzig2026]. The authors call these findings preliminary, since the ratings come from a model's reading of the transcripts and they cannot tell whether the code was used afterwards. In a randomised trial, 487 consultants at the firm BCG attempted data-science tasks outside their expertise, and those given ChatGPT outscored those given other resources. Among them, self-described competent coders came within about 5 percentage points of the firm's data scientists on the coding and statistics tasks, whereas the group as a whole stayed 12 to 14 points below them [@wiles2026]. Coding experience was not randomised, however, and the tool was a chat assistant.

Fluency in code does not guarantee independent judgement either. In another study from Anthropic, 50 professional analysts who regularly used R or Python carried out an analysis with Claude Code, whose preference on each decision had been secretly set by a coin flip. On four decisions between two reasonable options, they went with the agent's preference 86% of the time, and in an exploratory analysis, neither experience nor expertise predicted who did so [@herdagdelen2026]. The preferences were strengthened on purpose, so these figures may overstate everyday influence. The small group of less experienced analysts who chose to work without the agent made more serious errors, but because they chose for themselves, the comparison cannot isolate what the agent added.

Understanding is a further concern. In a small preprint, 54 computing students built a website, and those given a coding agent produced a better first version than those given a chatbot but understood it less well. With the agent, their background in code no longer predicted the quality of that version, but it still predicted their comprehension [@balepur2026]. An agent may therefore mask differences in literacy without removing them. Developers who learned a software package with AI assistance likewise understood it less well, and they were not significantly faster [@shen2026].

Research on automation explains why this matters. Automation leaves its operators to monitor the system and to take over when it fails, while the skills needed for both decay without practice [@bainbridge1983]. In a meta-analysis of 18 experiments, the more of a task that automation took over, the better performance was while it worked and the worse when it failed [@onnasch2014]. Complacency towards automation arises in experts as well as novices [@parasuraman2010]. Knowledge workers more confident in generative AI also reported less critical thinking [@lee2025], and Messeri and Crockett [-@messeri2024] warn that AI tools can leave scientists believing they understand more than they do. As agents improve, they give their supervisors fewer errors to catch, and so less practice at catching the ones that remain.

The evidence on learning is not uniform, since a meta-analysis of programming education found no reliable effect on exam scores, in either direction, when students could not use the tools in the exam [@maier2026]. What the website and package studies show is that the quality of the output and the understanding behind it need assessing separately. For researchers in training, I would still advise learning to read and write R or Python, which for now is the most direct way to check an agent's work. Study design, statistics and the habit of asking how a result could be wrong deserve at least as much of their time.

### What Experts Expect From Coding Agents

```{r forecast-data, include = FALSE}
# The Forecasting Research Institute's results for one question [fri2026tasks]: the year
# by which each panel's median forecast gave the milestone a 25%, 50% and 75% chance of
# having been reached
forecast_dates <- read.csv('data/expert-task-horizons.csv')
by_panel <- split(forecast_dates, forecast_dates$panel)
stopifnot(nrow(forecast_dates) == 6, setequal(names(by_panel), c('Experts', 'Superforecasters')),
          setequal(forecast_dates$probability, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75)),
          # in each panel, the years rise with the probability
          vapply(by_panel, function(d) !is.unsorted(d$year[order(d$probability)]), logical(1)))
year_of <- function(panel, probability) {
  sprintf('%.0f', forecast_dates$year[forecast_dates$panel == panel & forecast_dates$probability == probability])
}
even_chance <- c(Experts = year_of('Experts', 0.5), Superforecasters = year_of('Superforecasters', 0.5))

# One year is not a whole number, which the caption names
rounded <- forecast_dates$year != round(forecast_dates$year)
stopifnot(sum(rounded) == 1)
cap_forecasts <- sprintf(paste(
  'When Two Panels Expect a Model to Succeed 80%% of the Time at Eight-Hour Expert Tasks. The dots mark the years',
  'by which each panel\'s median forecast gave that milestone a 25%%, a 50%% (larger dot) and a 75%% chance of',
  'having been reached. They summarise each group\'s forecasts and are neither confidence intervals nor the',
  'spread between respondents. The %s\' year for a %s chance, %s, is shown rounded. Data from the',
  'results for the question [@fri2026tasks].'),
  tolower(forecast_dates$panel[rounded]), sprintf('%.0f%%', 100 * forecast_dates$probability[rounded]),
  format(forecast_dates$year[rounded], nsmall = 2))
alt_forecasts <- sprintf(paste(
  'Two rows of three dots on a time axis from 2026 to 2036. For a 25%%, 50%% and 75%% chance of the milestone,',
  'the experts\' median forecasts fall in %s, %s and %s, and the superforecasters\' in %s, %s and %s.'),
  year_of('Experts', 0.25), year_of('Experts', 0.5), year_of('Experts', 0.75),
  year_of('Superforecasters', 0.25), year_of('Superforecasters', 0.5), year_of('Superforecasters', 0.75))
```

This experiment captures one model on `r date_text(first_date)` and `r date_text(second_date)`, and each of its runs wrote one short script. Longer projects add a problem that these scripts did not test, the upkeep of a growing codebase, from its documentation to its stale and duplicated files. Carlini [-@carlini2026], who built a 100,000-line C compiler with 16 parallel agents, noted that 'LLM-written code frequently re-implements existing functionality' and assigned one agent to coalesce duplicate code and others to improve code quality and documentation. In SlopCodeBench, a benchmark in which agents repeatedly extend their own code, the code's structure eroded in 77% of the runs, and quality guidance repeated at every step improved the starting point without slowing the decline [@orlanski2026]. In open-source projects that adopted Cursor, an AI code editor, development sped up sharply but briefly, whereas static-analysis warnings and code complexity rose persistently [@he2026].

The upkeep is improving, if unevenly. In SWE-CI, a benchmark in which agents maintain real repositories over many rounds of change, each provider's newer models scored higher, although most models still broke previously passing tests in over three quarters of the tasks [@chen2026]. In a research note from the organisation METR, maintainers reviewing patches from successive models saw the step from Claude 4 Opus to Claude 4.5 Sonnet improve mostly code quality [@whitfill2026].

Experts have not forecast how long researchers will need to read code to check an agent's work, but their forecasts speak to a narrower milestone (Figure 4). In spring 2026, the Forecasting Research Institute asked its panels when a model would first succeed 80% of the time at tasks that take a human expert at least eight hours. The experts' median forecast gave that milestone an even chance by `r even_chance[['Experts']]`, and the superforecasters' by `r even_chance[['Superforecasters']]` [@fri2026tasks]. Those dates concern completing tasks, however, and say nothing directly about when agents will keep a codebase healthy without supervision, or when researchers can stop reading code.

```{r expert-forecasts, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 2.2, fig.cap = cap_forecasts, fig.alt = alt_forecasts}
# forecast_dates, read before the section's text, holds each panel's year for each
# probability. The bar joins a panel's years for a 25% and a 75% chance, which are
# group summaries, not a range of respondents' forecasts.
fig_forecasts <- function(narrow = FALSE, base_size = if (narrow) 12 else 11) {
  dates <- forecast_dates |>
    mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels = c('Superforecasters', 'Experts')),
           probability_label = sprintf('%.0f%%', 100 * probability),
           year_label = sprintf('%.0f', year))
  spans <- dates |> summarise(first = min(year), last = max(year), .by = panel)
  ggplot(dates, aes(year, panel)) +
    geom_segment(aes(x = first, xend = last, yend = panel), data = spans, colour = fig_roles[['grid']],
                 linewidth = 4.5, lineend = 'round') +
    geom_point(aes(size = probability == 0.5), colour = fig_roles[['ink']]) +
    # On a phone, a year is narrower than a label, so the outer labels lean outwards
    geom_text(aes(label = year_label,
                  hjust = if (narrow) c(0.8, 0.5, 0.2)[match(probability, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75))] else 0.5),
              nudge_y = -0.3, colour = fig_roles[['muted']], size = label_size(base_size)) +
    geom_text(aes(label = probability_label), data = filter(dates, panel == 'Experts'), nudge_y = 0.3,
              colour = fig_roles[['ink']], size = label_size(base_size)) +
    scale_size_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 2.2, `TRUE` = 3.6)) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2026, 2036, 2), limits = c(2026, 2036.4), expand = expansion(0)) +
    scale_y_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.55, 0.7))) +
    labs(x = if (narrow) 'Year'
             else 'Year by which the milestone has that probability of having been reached', y = NULL) +
    theme_figure(base_size) +
    theme(axis.text.y = element_text(colour = fig_roles[['ink']], size = rel(0.92)))
}
stopifnot(range(forecast_dates$year) >= 2026, range(forecast_dates$year) <= 2036)

draw_narrow(fig_forecasts(narrow = TRUE), width = 4.4, height = 2.7)
fig_forecasts()
```

Measurements of past progress point the same way. By METR's measure, the length of software task that frontier models can complete half the time doubled about every seven months between 2019 and 2025 [@kwa2025], and its update of January 2026 puts the doubling time since 2023 at about four months [@metr2026]. That measure has limits of its own. It rests on self-contained tasks 'with clear success criteria that can be automatically evaluated' [@metr-time-horizons], and by METR's account, relatively few of its tasks remain beyond the latest models [@metr2026]. The health of a codebase, by contrast, can be scored only in part. Agents resolved fewer tasks when they built on code written by other agents than on code written by people, and many traditional measures of maintainability did not explain the difference [@patel2026].

Capability need not turn into use, either. The computer scientists Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor [-@narayanan2025] distinguish gains in capability from the development and adoption of reliable applications. They expect diffusion to stay slow in consequential settings, held back by institutions, tacit knowledge and the need for validation, and a growing share of people's work to go into controlling AI. Upkeep illustrates their point, since whether a file is stale may depend on what its owner intends. Asked to 'clean up old branches', one agent issued a command to delete the branches on the remote server, although the user may have meant only those on their own computer [@hughes2026].

Whichever way these forecasts turn out, the case for saved and executed code would stand, since a script can be executed again whether or not anyone reads it. A well-kept codebase can still implement a poor analysis, and whether an effect should be allowed to vary across words depends on what a study means to generalise to, which no amount of tidying settles. Someone also has to answer for the result, which is why *Nature* decided in 2023 to accept no language model as a credited author [@nature2023]. In the meantime, the practical question is how to check the work that agents produce.

### A Workflow for Research With Coding Agents

The experiment and the wider evidence point to a workflow built on the three choices reviewed at the start, the tools, the requests and the record, with checking and upkeep between them.

The tools come first, and their choice deserves a reason. I used a proprietary model because its behaviour was the object of study, a case in which @mcloughlin2026 suggest that the choice may be reasonable [see also @palmer2024]. Where a model's replies are themselves the data, as in text annotation, a model whose version can be fixed, such as an open model run locally, gives a far stronger record [@spirling2023]. With real data, the terms of consent and data protection also need checking before an agent sends anything it reads to a hosted model.

An analysis plan written before any code, ideally in a preregistration, allows every request to be a specified one, and the request can also ask for a runnable script, pinned dependencies and tests. Where a decision remains open, it may help to form a view before seeing the agent's preference, or to ask it for the best case for each option, two approaches that @herdagdelen2026 suggest exploring.

Checking falls, for now, to someone who reads each change before accepting it and executes each script again in a fresh R process. That includes what the code does to files, since `r count_text(sum(!results$compliant[script_runs]), sum(script_runs))` of the `r count_text(sum(script_runs))` script agents of the first round wrote outside their folders. A growing project soon outruns any reader, and the checking then has to rest on independent reanalysis and on tests with many simulated data sets whose answers are known [@morris2019]. One data set would not have been enough here, since both intervals of the second round's open-request scripts contain the population effect (Figure 3), and only many data sets would show how often each misses it. Tests alone are not enough either. Maintainers of three open-source projects would not have merged roughly half of the patches by agents of 2024 and 2025 that had passed a benchmark's tests, although those agents had no chance to respond to feedback [@whitfill2026].

The upkeep belongs in that review. After each substantial change, the documentation, stale files, inconsistencies and duplicated code all need a look. An agent can take on much of this work, as in Carlini's project [@carlini2026], but asking it to may not be enough, since repeated guidance did not slow the decline in SlopCodeBench [@orlanski2026].

Finally, the record should include the effort level, alongside the versions of the model and the agentic tool, the settings, the prompts, the replies, the tool calls, the scripts and their outputs, and the software environment [@baltes2026; @feuerriegel2026]. Having left the first round's effort level unrecorded, I can only hint at its part in the differences between the rounds.

Used in this way, coding agents can make an AI-assisted analysis far more reproducible than a reply written without running code. Their summaries of their own work, however, are more text from the same model, so for now, the checking falls to a researcher who can specify, read and execute the code. How long that will hold is the least certain part of this post. That someone will have to answer for the result is among the most certain.
